The Office of the Attorney General's Consumer Protection Division oversees and investigates certain consumer disputes involving common ownership communities and was consulted for the fiscal analysis.
The Secretary of State oversees registration and records relating to certain common ownership communities and housing disclosures and served as an information source for the bill.

qa_results.bill_summary: This bill shifts the annual reporting requirement regarding charges, convictions, and sentences for specific handgun and regulated firearm violations from the State Commission on Criminal Sentencing Policy to the Maryland Judiciary. Reports must be submitted annually by October 1 to the Governor and the General Assembly, with data disaggregated by jurisdiction, race, and gender.
qa_results.responsible_party: Maryland Judiciary
qa_results.stakeholders: Maryland Judiciary, State Commission on Criminal Sentencing Policy, state policymakers, and individuals charged with or convicted of regulated firearm violations.
qa_results.fiscal_impact_summary: The Maryland Judiciary can fulfill the bill's reporting requirements using existing budgeted resources. State revenues are not affected, and local government operations and finances are not anticipated to be materially affected.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: HB 315 designates the Maryland Judiciary (administratively supported by the Administrative Office of the Courts) as the entity responsible for compiling and submitting an annual report to the Governor and the General Assembly detailing charges, convictions, and sentences for specified regulated firearm violations disaggregated by jurisdiction, race, and gender.
The bill mandates that the annual report on charges, convictions, and sentences for specified firearm violations be submitted directly to the Governor on or before October 1 of each year.

qa_results.bill_summary: Adds the Secretary of Emergency Management and the Chair of the Public Service Commission, or their respective designees, as members of the Maryland Commission on Climate Change.
qa_results.responsible_party: Maryland Commission on Climate Change
qa_results.stakeholders: Members of the Maryland Commission on Climate Change, the Maryland Department of Emergency Management, and the Public Service Commission.
qa_results.fiscal_impact_summary: State effect is minimal; any expense reimbursements for additional commission members are assumed to be minimal and absorbable within existing budgeted resources. There is no local or small business fiscal impact.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: House Bill 323 directly adds the Secretary of Emergency Management, or the Secretary's designee, as an official member of the Maryland Commission on Climate Change.
House Bill 323 directly adds the Chair of the Public Service Commission, or the Chair's designee, as an official member of the Maryland Commission on Climate Change.
The Maryland Commission on Climate Change is statutorily established within the Department of the Environment, which also jointly staffs and supports the Commission.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Executive Commissions, Committees, Task Forces, and Advisory Boards
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill amends the statutory composition and membership requirements of an executive advisory body, the Maryland Commission on Climate Change.
The Department of Natural Resources jointly staffs the Maryland Commission on Climate Change alongside the Department of the Environment.

qa_results.bill_summary: This bill increases the threshold monetary amount from $10,000 to $25,000 above which certain transfers made by a personal representative, trustee, or conservator to a custodian for the benefit of a minor under the Maryland Uniform Transfers to Minors Act require court authorization.
qa_results.responsible_party: Maryland Judiciary and Orphans' Courts
qa_results.stakeholders: Minors receiving transferred assets, along with personal representatives, trustees, conservators, and custodians managing property for minors
qa_results.fiscal_impact_summary: The bill does not materially affect State or local government finances.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill increases the monetary threshold required for court authorization of certain transfers to a custodian for a minor made by personal representatives, trustees, or conservators. The Register of Wills administers probate proceedings and serves as clerk to the Orphans' Court, which oversees these fiduciary appointments and estate administration matters.

The bill alters the threshold amount that triggers the requirement for court authorization of custodial transfers for minors under the Maryland Uniform Transfers to Minors Act, directly affecting judicial case processing and petitions submitted to the courts.

qa_results.bill_summary: Alters the statutory definition of an 'interested person' in estate and trust administration to exclude legatees whose interests have been fully adeemed, include surviving spouses who timely elect an elective share and individuals who timely petition to caveat a will, and explicitly exclude assignees of a legatee or heir.
qa_results.responsible_party: Maryland Registers of Wills and Orphans' Courts
qa_results.stakeholders: Heirs, legatees, surviving spouses electing an elective share, individuals filing a caveat to contest a will, assignees of heirs or legatees, personal representatives, and probate estate administrators.
qa_results.fiscal_impact_summary: The bill does not materially affect State or local government finances.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The Register of Wills oversees the administrative probate of decedents' estates and acts as clerk to the Orphans' Court. The bill directly alters who qualifies as an 'interested person' entitled to receive notices and file petitions with the Register of Wills during probate administration.

The Administrative Office of the Courts supports the Maryland Judicial Branch. The bill affects judicial probate, caveat proceedings, and court determinations regarding elective shares and interested party standing in estate and trust litigation.

qa_results.bill_summary: Limits who may object to the appointment of a personal representative of a decedent's estate by modifying the published notice of appointment to specify that only interested persons or unpaid claimants, rather than any person, are authorized to file an objection.
qa_results.responsible_party: Registers of Wills
qa_results.stakeholders: Personal representatives, estate beneficiaries, heirs, executors, and unpaid claimants or creditors of decedents' estates.
qa_results.fiscal_impact_summary: The bill does not materially affect State or local government finances.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: HB 326 directly governs the required notice that the Register of Wills publishes upon the appointment of a personal representative and specifies who may file objections to the appointment with the Register.

The Administrative Office of the Courts provides administrative and legal support to the judicial branch, including the Orphans' Court where disputed estate matters and objections to appointments are adjudicated.

qa_results.bill_summary: This bill increases the membership of the Board of Community College Trustees for Anne Arundel County from 8 to 10 members. It also requires the Governor, to the extent practicable, to take into consideration the geographic and ethnic representation of Anne Arundel County when making appointments to ensure all segments of the county's population are represented.
qa_results.responsible_party: Governor of Maryland
qa_results.stakeholders: Anne Arundel Community College, residents of Anne Arundel County, and prospective board trustees
qa_results.fiscal_impact_summary: The bill has no State fiscal impact. Local expenditures for Anne Arundel Community College increase minimally starting in fiscal 2025 for onboarding costs (a one-time cost of $1,500), annual travel reimbursements (up to $3,000 per trustee annually), and software access ($400 per trustee annually), which are expected to be absorbed with existing resources. College revenues are unaffected.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill directly requires the Governor to appoint two additional members to the Board of Community College Trustees for Anne Arundel County and mandates that the Governor consider geographic and ethnic representation when making these appointments.

As the unit within the Executive Department responsible for recruiting, vetting, and managing gubernatorial appointments to state and local boards and commissions, the Office of Appointments will facilitate the selection and processing of the two new trustees.

As the state's coordinating board for postsecondary education, changes to the governance and board structure of Maryland community colleges are relevant to MHEC's overall oversight of higher education institutions.
As the coordinating body for postsecondary education in Maryland, governance changes to community college boards fall within its broader subject matter jurisdiction.

qa_results.bill_summary: Revises requirements for hospital financial assistance policies by permitting hospitals to consider only household monetary assets in excess of $100,000 (while excluding specified retirement assets) when determining patient eligibility for free and reduced-cost care, and removes the condition that reduced-cost care and payment plans must be in accordance with the hospital's mission and service area.
qa_results.responsible_party: Health Services Cost Review Commission
qa_results.stakeholders: Uninsured and low-income hospital patients, acute care and chronic care hospitals, and health payers in Maryland
qa_results.fiscal_impact_summary: Any additional administrative workload for the Health Services Cost Review Commission will be managed with existing budgeted resources. Fiscal impacts on Maryland Department of Health chronic care hospitals and overall uncompensated care are indeterminate but expected to be minimal. To the extent hospital rates increase due to changes in uncompensated care, Medicaid expenditures (39% general funds, 61% federal funds) and federal matching revenues could increase beginning as early as FY 2025. No local government fiscal impact.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: HSCRC oversees acute and chronic care hospitals in Maryland and establishes the regulatory framework for hospital rates, uncompensated care pools, and hospital financial assistance policies. The bill amends the statutory requirements for hospital financial assistance policies under HSCRC's jurisdiction.

MDH operates state chronic care hospitals (such as Western Maryland Hospital Center and Deer's Head Hospital Center) that must comply with the modified financial assistance and asset test policies. Additionally, MDH administers the Medicaid program, which may experience an expenditure impact if hospital rates adjust due to changes in uncompensated care.

qa_results.bill_summary: Requires the Motor Vehicle Administration (MVA), in consultation with Baltimore City and other interested jurisdictions, to prepare and submit a comprehensive report by December 1, 2024, regarding motor vehicles owned by Maryland residents that are improperly titled or registered in other states.
qa_results.responsible_party: Maryland Motor Vehicle Administration (MVA)
qa_results.stakeholders: Maryland motor vehicle owners (specifically those with vehicles titled or registered in other states), local governments including Baltimore City, and state transportation and enforcement agencies.
qa_results.fiscal_impact_summary: State and local expenditures are not materially affected, as the Motor Vehicle Administration and participating local jurisdictions can complete the study and report using existing resources. State and local revenues are unaffected.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: HB 332 directly mandates the Motor Vehicle Administration (MVA), in consultation with Baltimore City and other jurisdictions, to research, prepare, and submit a comprehensive report regarding Maryland residents improperly registering vehicles out of state.

As the parent department of the Motor Vehicle Administration, the Department of Transportation oversees the policies, resources, and administrative implementation associated with state vehicle registration and compliance reporting.
The bill requires the Motor Vehicle Administration to submit its final report of findings and policy recommendations directly to the Governor by December 1, 2024.

qa_results.bill_summary: Requires the State Board of Elections to maintain a website portal where the public can report election misinformation and disinformation, periodically review submissions to issue corrective information or make referrals to the State Prosecutor, and defines 'influence' regarding voting interference prohibitions to include pressure, deception, trickery, or authority.
qa_results.responsible_party: Maryland State Board of Elections
qa_results.stakeholders: Maryland voters, the general public, and individuals subject to election law enforcement
qa_results.fiscal_impact_summary: State general fund expenditures increase by at least $50,000 in FY 2024 (or FY 2025) for the State Board of Elections to create the website reporting portal. Special fund revenues for the Fair Campaign Financing Fund may increase annually beginning in FY 2025 from civil or criminal penalty collections. There is no local fiscal impact.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The Maryland State Board of Elections is the primary implementing agency tasked with establishing and maintaining a public reporting portal on its website for election misinformation and disinformation, reviewing submissions periodically, publishing corrective information, and referring appropriate cases to the State Prosecutor.

The Office of the State Prosecutor investigates and prosecutes election law violations in Maryland and is explicitly designated in the statute to receive case referrals from the State Board of Elections regarding election disinformation and improper voter influence.
The Administrative Office of the Courts oversees the court system where misdemeanor and civil penalty charges under the amended improper voter influence provisions would be adjudicated.

qa_results.bill_summary: Alters the geographic boundary in the 45th alcoholic beverages district of Baltimore City within which Class B-D-7 beer, wine, and liquor license holders and certain other specified licensees are restricted to operating between 9:00 a.m. and 10:00 p.m.
qa_results.responsible_party: Baltimore City Board of License Commissioners
qa_results.stakeholders: Class B-D-7 license holders, other affected alcoholic beverage licensees, businesses, and residents located within the redefined boundaries of the 45th alcoholic beverages district in Baltimore City.
qa_results.fiscal_impact_summary: State finances are not affected. Baltimore City can manage any additional enforcement using existing resources, and local revenues are not affected.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The Comptroller of Maryland regulates the state's alcohol industry. While this legislation alters local hours of sale and geographic boundaries for specific retail licenses in Baltimore City—which are primarily administered and enforced by the local Baltimore City Board of License Commissioners with no state fiscal impact—it pertains to the broader statutory framework governing alcoholic beverage regulation in Maryland.

qa_results.bill_summary: Requires the Maryland State Treasurer to develop written informational materials regarding the Maryland Achieving a Better Life Experience (ABLE) Program and provide them to the State Board of Education and local school systems. It further requires local school systems to distribute these materials, in the parents' native language if necessary, to parents during Individualized Education Program (IEP), Individualized Family Service Plan (IFSP), and Section 504 plan meetings.
qa_results.responsible_party: Maryland State Treasurer, Maryland State Department of Education (MSDE), and local boards of education
qa_results.stakeholders: Children with disabilities, their parents or legal guardians participating in IEP, IFSP, or 504 plan meetings, and local school systems
qa_results.fiscal_impact_summary: State general fund revenues and local revenues decrease, potentially significantly, beginning in FY 2025 as new ABLE accounts lead to increased personal income tax subtraction modifications (estimated at a loss of $137,500 in State revenues and $88,500 in local revenues per 1,000 additional filers). State Treasurer nonbudgeted fee revenues and distribution expenditures increase from new accounts. MSDE expenditures increase minimally in FY 2025 for tracking system enhancements, while local school systems can distribute materials with existing resources.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: HB 336 explicitly requires the State Treasurer to develop written informational materials regarding the Maryland ABLE Program (in both electronic and physical formats, including translated versions) and provide them to the State Board of Education and local school boards. The Treasurer also administers the Maryland ABLE Program.

The bill requires the State Board of Education and local school systems to receive and distribute ABLE Program informational materials to parents at IEP, IFSP, and Section 504 plan meetings. MSDE is tasked with regulatory oversight and system enhancements to track distribution compliance.
Maryland 529 encompasses the Maryland ABLE Program whose materials and enrollment are directly targeted and expanded by this legislation.

The Comptroller manages state income tax collection and is fiscally impacted by reductions in general fund revenues resulting from additional subtraction modifications claimed for contributions to and distributions from newly created ABLE accounts.

qa_results.bill_summary: The Sarah Debbink Langenkamp Memorial Act establishes enhanced penalties for a driver of a motor vehicle who fails to yield the right-of-way to a person lawfully riding a bicycle, electric personal assistive mobility device (EPAMD), or motor scooter in a designated bike lane or shoulder if the violation contributes to serious physical injury or death. Violators face up to two months of imprisonment, a fine of up to $2,000, or both.
qa_results.responsible_party: Maryland Judiciary
qa_results.stakeholders: Motor vehicle drivers, bicyclists, motor scooter operators, and electric personal assistive mobility device (EPAMD) riders.
qa_results.fiscal_impact_summary: State general fund expenditures for the Judiciary increase by $56,900 in FY 2025 only for programming updates. The bill is not expected to materially affect local finances or operations.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The Judiciary incurs a direct fiscal impact of $56,900 in FY 2025 to implement necessary computer programming updates for the new violation and penalty structure in District and circuit court systems.
The bill directly amends Title 21 of the Transportation Article governing vehicle operations, right-of-way rules, and bicycle safety on state roadways.
The MVA records traffic convictions, maintains driver histories, and assesses driving record points for moving violations and crashes under Title 21 of the Transportation Article.

As the primary state law enforcement agency enforcing motor vehicle laws on Maryland highways, MSP officers are responsible for enforcing right-of-way laws and investigating collisions involving serious physical injury or death.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Maryland Office of the Public Defender
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: Because the bill establishes a penalty of up to two months imprisonment for this violation, indigent defendants charged under the statute become eligible for legal representation through OPD.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Department of Public Safety and Correctional Services
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The department oversees state correctional and detention operations and was consulted as an information source regarding the bill's incarceration penalties of up to two months.
MDOT SHA plans, designs, and maintains state roadway infrastructure, including designated bike lanes and paved shoulders where these right-of-way provisions apply.

qa_results.bill_summary: Establishes statewide standards, restrictions, and procedures for the use of facial recognition technology by law enforcement agencies in criminal investigations. The bill limits facial recognition searches to certain serious offenses, prohibits real-time surveillance and searches based solely on protected characteristics, restricts the admissibility of results in court proceedings, mandates independent human verification, and requires agency auditing, public reporting, and annual training.
qa_results.responsible_party: Department of State Police and the Department of Public Safety and Correctional Services
qa_results.stakeholders: State and local law enforcement agencies, criminal defendants, juveniles in delinquency proceedings, crime victims, and the general public
qa_results.fiscal_impact_summary: State general fund expenditures increase by at least $474,149 in FY 2025, which reflects $442,966 and 5 positions for the Department of Public Safety and Correctional Services to build and administer a mandatory training program, and $31,183 and 0.5 positions for the Governor's Office of Crime Prevention, Youth, and Victim Services to manage annual reporting. Future ongoing expenditures range from $508,800 in FY 2026 to $579,200 in FY 2029. Local law enforcement agencies will incur operational impacts and potential costs related to compliance and training. Revenues are unaffected.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Department of Public Safety and Correctional Services
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: DPSCS is mandated by the bill to develop and administer an annual statewide training program regarding facial recognition technology for law enforcement officers by June 30, 2026, and to independently verify results; it also operates the Maryland Image Repository System (MIRS) and incurs significant fiscal expenditure for staff and training systems.

The Department of State Police is statutorily required to adopt and publish the model statewide policy governing the use of facial recognition technology across all Maryland law enforcement agencies and must comply with the operational, training, audit, and reporting mandates.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Governor's Office of Crime Prevention and Policy
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: GOCPP is required to receive annual FRT use reports from every law enforcement agency by May 1 and compile, disaggregate, and submit a comprehensive annual report to the Governor and the General Assembly by October 1, requiring additional staff funding.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Maryland Office of the Public Defender
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: OPD represents criminal and juvenile defendants directly affected by the bill's new mandatory discovery disclosures, strict evidentiary prohibitions on FRT results, and is specifically granted statutory authority to request copies of law enforcement FRT compliance audits.

MVA's database of driver's license and identification card photographs is specifically designated by the bill as one of the primary authorized databases law enforcement may search using facial recognition technology.

The Judiciary is directly responsible for enforcing the bill's restrictions on the admissibility of FRT evidence in preliminary hearings, warrant applications, and juvenile delinquency cases, and adjudicating civil actions brought to compel agency compliance.

The OAG is explicitly authorized to request and review law enforcement agency annual FRT audit records and may be involved in advising state agencies and representing them in civil actions filed under the subtitle.

MDOT oversees the Motor Vehicle Administration whose photo database is utilized for searches, as well as modal law enforcement divisions (such as the MTA Police) that must comply with FRT operational, auditing, and training requirements.

DNR operates the Maryland Natural Resources Police, a state law enforcement agency subject to the bill's requirements regarding FRT investigative limits, mandatory training, auditing, and annual reporting.
DGS operates the Maryland Capitol Police, which is subject to the bill's standards, restrictions, training, auditing, and reporting mandates on the use of facial recognition technology.

qa_results.bill_summary: Extends the State's prompt payment requirements and dispute resolution framework for State procurement contracts to include suppliers who provide labor or materials to prime contractors, requiring contractors to pay undisputed amounts owed to suppliers within 10 days of receiving payment from the State.
qa_results.responsible_party: State procurement officers and procurement units across Maryland State agencies
qa_results.stakeholders: Suppliers of labor and materials for State contracts, prime contractors holding State procurement contracts, subcontractors, and State procurement officers.
qa_results.fiscal_impact_summary: There is no state or local fiscal impact. State agencies can implement the bill's requirements using existing budgeted resources, and there is no effect on state revenues. Local governments are unaffected because the bill applies only to State procurement contracts.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: As the state's central procurement authority, DGS is directly responsible for procurement policies, drafting standard contract provisions, and managing procurement officers who must administer and enforce the new prompt payment and dispute resolution requirements for suppliers.

The Board of Public Works establishes state procurement regulations and approves major state contracts, which will need to incorporate the updated statutory requirements regarding prompt payment to suppliers.

MDOT administers extensive capital and infrastructure construction contracts that heavily utilize material and labor suppliers, requiring its procurement officers and project managers to comply with and enforce the prompt payment dispute process.
DBM exercises central administrative and fiscal oversight over state procurement, contract administration, and state budgeting processes impacted by procurement terms.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Maryland State Board of Contract Appeals
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: MSBCA adjudicates state contract disputes and bid protests; while the bill specifies that certain procurement officer decisions under this section are not subject to standard administrative appeals under Part III of the subtitle, the clarification directly affects the board's jurisdictional boundaries.

USM operates under independent procurement authority for its capital projects and facilities, requiring its procurement personnel to update contract templates and adhere to the prompt payment framework for suppliers.

qa_results.bill_summary: House Bill 343 authorizes the Maryland Department of the Environment (MDE) and the Board of Public Works (BPW) to approve the redeposit of dredged material from large redevelopment sites at the Hart-Miller Island Dredged Material Containment Facility through December 31, 2027, subject to an enforceable community benefits agreement with Baltimore County. The bill also authorizes MDE to approve contained areas for dredge material at large redevelopment sites, expands the duties of the Hart-Miller-Pleasure Island Citizens Oversight Committee, and alters the membership and duties of the Cox Creek Citizens Oversight Committee.
qa_results.responsible_party: Maryland Department of the Environment
qa_results.stakeholders: Communities and residents near Hart-Miller Island and Cox Creek (Anne Arundel and Baltimore counties), commercial port developers (such as Tradepoint Atlantic at Sparrows Point), environmental and recreational conservation organizations, and local watermen and birders.
qa_results.fiscal_impact_summary: State finances could be impacted if the Hart-Miller Island facility is reopened under State management; the Maryland Port Administration estimated initial reopening costs between $7,000,000 and $9,000,000 and annual operating costs of roughly $6,500,000, though costs would be offset by per-cubic-yard containment fees charged to the entity depositing material. Baltimore County revenues may increase significantly through a required community benefits agreement, with equal county expenditures dedicated to local community benefits.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill grants MDE statutory authority to approve contained areas at large redevelopment sites and to approve the redeposit of dredged material at the Hart-Miller Island Dredged Material Containment Facility under specified conditions.

The bill directly amends statute to require the Cox Creek Citizens Oversight Committee to advise, provide feedback, and make recommendations to MPA regarding dredged material management, and MPA oversees the State's Dredged Material Management Program and placement sites.
The bill explicitly authorizes BPW to approve a license or an amendment to a license authorizing the deposit of dredged material at the Hart-Miller Island Dredged Material Containment Facility.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Executive Commissions, Committees, Task Forces, and Advisory Boards
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The legislation directly alters the statutory membership, functions, and oversight responsibilities of both the Cox Creek Citizens Oversight Committee and the Hart-Miller-Pleasure Island Citizens Oversight Committee.

MDOT is the parent agency of the Maryland Port Administration and is directly involved in dredging policy, navigation channels, and infrastructure support for port-related dredged material management.
DNR owns Hart-Miller Island and operates a State park on the southern portion of the island, which could see operational and fiscal impacts if the dredged material containment facility reopens.
The Governor is responsible for appointing members and establishing terms for both the Cox Creek Citizens Oversight Committee and the Hart-Miller-Pleasure Island Citizens Oversight Committee.
The Office of Appointments assists the Governor in recruiting, vetting, and administering appointments for the altered seats on the Citizens Oversight Committees.
MES provides technical and operational support under contract to MPA for the Dredged Material Management Program and placement facilities.

qa_results.bill_summary: This bill updates the Endangered Species of Fish Conservation Act and the Nongame and Endangered Species Conservation Act by establishing statutory requirements for petitions to list or delist endangered or threatened species. It requires the Secretary of Natural Resources to review and, if warranted, update regulations listing endangered and threatened species by July 1, 2026, and at least every five years thereafter, and expands the definitions of 'fish' and 'wildlife' to include invertebrates and products derived from them.
qa_results.responsible_party: Maryland Department of Natural Resources (Secretary of Natural Resources)
qa_results.stakeholders: Wildlife conservationists, scientific researchers, individuals or organizations petitioning to list or unlist species, and regulated entities interacting with native fish and wildlife.
qa_results.fiscal_impact_summary: State and local finances are not affected. The Department of Natural Resources can implement the requirements using existing budgeted resources.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill directly modifies titles within the Natural Resources Article under the Department of Natural Resources' (DNR) purview, requiring the Secretary of Natural Resources to review and update endangered and threatened species listings at least every five years, altering statutory definitions of 'fish' and 'wildlife', and codifying petition requirements for listing or delisting species.

qa_results.bill_summary: House Bill 353 updates the definition of the Health and Human Services Referral System to encompass a coordinated statewide system accessible via 2-1-1 and other modern technology systems rather than solely telephone service. It repeals requirements that the Maryland Department of Health evaluate the performance of individual 2-1-1 call centers or recommend corrective actions, and it expresses legislative intent for 2-1-1 Maryland to add two call center representatives to its board of directors.
qa_results.responsible_party: Maryland Department of Health
qa_results.stakeholders: Maryland residents seeking health and human services resources, 2-1-1 Maryland, and 2-1-1 call centers
qa_results.fiscal_impact_summary: According to the Fiscal Note, any change in State activities does not materially affect State finances, and there is no local fiscal impact.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill directly amends the statutory responsibilities of the Maryland Department of Health by repealing requirements that it evaluate the performance of 2-1-1 call centers, make recommendations on service quality, and recommend corrective actions.

As the primary state department administering human services programs, DHS coordinates with the Health and Human Services Referral System and is subject to consultation requirements regarding public hotlines and referral services.

qa_results.bill_summary: Establishes the Workgroup on Health and Wellness in Prince George's County to evaluate local health and wellness practices, healthy eating initiatives, and access to recreation, and to make recommendations regarding community programming, incentives, and integrative health hubs.
qa_results.responsible_party: Prince George's County Health Department
qa_results.stakeholders: Prince George's County residents, local businesses, health and wellness practitioners, and county government agencies
qa_results.fiscal_impact_summary: State operations and finances are not affected. Prince George's County expenditures increase by approximately $120,000 in FY 2025 and FY 2026 to hire one contractual employee to provide staff support for the workgroup and draft the required report. County revenues are unaffected.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Executive Commissions, Committees, Task Forces, and Advisory Boards
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: House Bill 358 creates a statutory, temporary Workgroup on Health and Wellness in Prince George's County tasked with evaluating health practices, integrative programs, and community wellness, and reporting its recommendations.
The bill mandates that the Workgroup submit its final report of findings and recommendations to the Governor on or before December 1, 2025.

qa_results.bill_summary: Establishes a barbershop and beauty salon beer and wine license in Caroline County, allowing licensed establishments to provide customers up to 12 ounces of beer or 5 ounces of wine by the glass for on-premises consumption while receiving barbering or cosmetology services.
qa_results.responsible_party: Caroline County Board of License Commissioners
qa_results.stakeholders: Barbershop and beauty salon owners, employees, and customers in Caroline County.
qa_results.fiscal_impact_summary: State finances are not materially affected. Caroline County local revenues will increase minimally by $100 annually for each new license issued, and any enforcement or inspection responsibilities can be absorbed with existing local resources.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill conditions eligibility for the Caroline County alcoholic beverages license on holding a valid barbershop permit (§ 4-501) or beauty salon permit (§ 5-501) issued under the Business Occupations and Professions Article, which are regulated and issued by licensing boards within the Maryland Department of Labor.

The Comptroller of Maryland oversees the regulation of the alcoholic beverage industry and enforcement of state alcoholic beverage laws and excise taxes, though local administration of this license is handled directly by the Caroline County Board of License Commissioners.

qa_results.bill_summary: Expands Caroline County's existing one-day beer and wine tasting license to include liquor, creating a one-day beer, wine, and liquor tasting (BWLT) license. It updates eligibility requirements to include organizations qualifying for Class C per diem licenses, raises the daily tasting limit for beer from 8 to 9 ounces, and establishes tasting limits for liquor at 0.5 ounces per offering and up to 2.5 ounces per day.
qa_results.responsible_party: Caroline County Board of License Commissioners
qa_results.stakeholders: Nonprofit organizations, clubs, alcohol license holders, and event attendees participating in alcohol tasting events in Caroline County.
qa_results.fiscal_impact_summary: The bill has no state fiscal impact. It is not anticipated to materially affect Caroline County operations or finances, as the $50 license fee remains unchanged and small business impacts are minimal.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The Comptroller of Maryland regulates the alcoholic beverage industry across the state. While this bill pertains specifically to local licensing administered by the Caroline County Board of License Commissioners with no state fiscal impact, statutory alterations to alcoholic beverage tasting licenses fall broadly within the Comptroller's regulatory domain.

qa_results.bill_summary: Authorizes the use of up to 10 stop sign monitoring systems in school zones on State and local highways in Prince George's County, subject to local approval. The bill subjects vehicle owners or drivers failing to stop at monitored stop signs to a civil penalty up to $40, establishes defenses, sets citation and trial procedures under District Court jurisdiction, and requires Prince George's County to submit an implementation and safety effectiveness report by December 1, 2025.
qa_results.responsible_party: Prince George's County (including the Prince George's County Department of Public Works and Transportation and local law enforcement agencies), the District Court of Maryland, and the Maryland State Highway Administration.
qa_results.stakeholders: Motorists and vehicle owners traveling through school zones in Prince George's County, students, pedestrians, Prince George's County local governments, and law enforcement agencies.
qa_results.fiscal_impact_summary: State general fund expenditures increase by approximately $11,100 in FY 2025 only for District Court computer programming changes. State general fund revenues may increase indeterminately from FY 2025 through FY 2029 from fines collected by the District Court for contested citations. Transportation Trust Fund expenditures may increase if systems are placed on State highways requiring signage. Local revenues and expenditures in Prince George's County will increase from FY 2025 through FY 2029 depending on deployment; revenues from civil penalties (up to $40) are dedicated solely to public safety purposes, while local expenditures will cover system start-up and operating costs.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The District Court has exclusive original civil jurisdiction over contested citations issued under the bill. The Chief Judge of the District Court must adopt trial and citation procedures, prescribe a uniform citation form, and set prepayment penalties. Additionally, the court system incurs $11,100 in FY 2025 computer programming costs.

Stop sign monitoring systems deployed on State highways in Prince George's County school zones require approval from SHA, and SHA is statutorily required to install prominent warning signage on State highways where systems are utilized.
MVA is authorized to refuse or suspend motor vehicle registrations for unpaid and uncontested citations, and is prohibited from assessing points or recording these violations on driving records.
As the parent agency of SHA and MVA, MDOT's Transportation Trust Fund finances expenditures associated with signage installation and any State highway oversight under the program.
The Prince George's County Department of Public Works and Transportation is required to submit a comprehensive implementation, cost, and effectiveness report to the Governor by December 1, 2025.

qa_results.bill_summary: Requires each community college in Maryland, in consultation with students and student organizations, to develop and implement a plan by August 1, 2025, to provide students with access to over-the-counter contraception on campus, and mandates annual reporting on plan implementation to the Maryland Higher Education Commission, which will report to the General Assembly.
qa_results.responsible_party: Maryland Higher Education Commission, Maryland Department of Health, and Maryland community colleges
qa_results.stakeholders: Community college students and Maryland community college administrations
qa_results.fiscal_impact_summary: Baltimore City Community College (BCCC) and local community college expenditures may increase, especially in FY 2025 and FY 2026 for one-time set-up costs like purchasing vending machines; however, specific dollar estimates are not provided in the Fiscal Note. Higher education revenues may increase minimally to offset costs if fees are charged to students. The Maryland Department of Health can provide plan development assistance within existing budgeted resources.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill requires each community college to submit an annual report to the Maryland Higher Education Commission on the implementation of its over-the-counter contraception plan, and requires the Commission to compile and submit an annual report to the General Assembly.

The Maryland Higher Education Commission is mandated to receive annual implementation reports on over-the-counter contraception plans from community colleges and submit an annual report on the findings to the General Assembly.

The bill authorizes the Maryland Department of Health, upon request, to assist community colleges in developing over-the-counter contraception plans and in collaborating with organizations experienced in vending machine distribution.

qa_results.bill_summary: Establishes uniform procedures for election recounts in Maryland by requiring a petitioner to select one of three approved recount methods (rescanning ballots, manually recounting voter-verifiable paper records, or another method approved by the State Administrator) and requiring local boards of elections to preserve, store, and review duplicate ballots alongside their corresponding voter-verifiable paper records.
qa_results.responsible_party: Maryland State Board of Elections and local boards of elections
qa_results.stakeholders: Election candidates, registered voters petitioning for recounts, and local election administrators and election judges
qa_results.fiscal_impact_summary: The bill is not expected to materially affect State or local government finances.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill directly governs election administration by defining permitted recount methods and procedures for handling duplicate ballots and voter-verifiable paper records, specifically granting authority to the State Board of Elections and State Administrator regarding equipment feasibility and method approvals.

qa_results.bill_summary: Establishes the Rent Court Workforce Solutions Pilot Program in Montgomery County and Prince George's County to provide residential tenants facing failure to pay rent proceedings with workforce resources, information on workforce development, registered apprenticeships, and employment opportunities.
qa_results.responsible_party: Designated organizations (fiscal and administrative agents of the local workforce development boards in Montgomery and Prince George's counties), in coordination with the District Court and the Maryland Department of Labor
qa_results.stakeholders: Residential tenants facing failure to pay rent eviction proceedings in Montgomery County and Prince George's County, local workforce development boards, and District Court personnel.
qa_results.fiscal_impact_summary: State general fund expenditures increase by $200,000 annually beginning in FY 2026. This reflects a mandated annual appropriation of $100,000 each to the designated organizations in Montgomery County and Prince George's County for FY 2026 through FY 2028, with discretionary spending assumed beyond FY 2028. State revenues are not affected, and there is no direct fiscal impact on local government operations or finances.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill directly involves District Court courthouses in Montgomery County and Prince George's County, authorizing administrative judges to enter into Memoranda of Understanding to allow representatives from designated workforce organizations to operate within courthouses during failure to pay rent proceedings.

The pilot program focuses on connecting covered individuals in rent court to workforce development programs, registered apprenticeships, and employment opportunities, and the fiscal note assumes the mandated state funding will be appropriated within the Maryland Department of Labor's budget for disbursement to the local designated organizations.

The bill creates a statutory mandated appropriation of $200,000 annually from general funds for fiscal years 2026 through 2028 that must be incorporated into the Governor's executive budget developed by DBM.

The Governor is statutorily mandated to include $200,000 in annual appropriations for the pilot program in the state budget bills for fiscal years 2026 through 2028 and will receive annual reports regarding program outcomes starting January 1, 2026.

qa_results.bill_summary: Renames statutory references to the Port of Baltimore throughout the Annotated Code of Maryland to the Helen Delich Bentley Port of Baltimore.
qa_results.responsible_party: Maryland Department of Transportation / Maryland Port Administration
qa_results.stakeholders: Maritime industry, port workers, shipping companies, and businesses operating in or using the Helen Delich Bentley Port of Baltimore
qa_results.fiscal_impact_summary: The bill has no state or local fiscal impact, as it is purely technical in nature and codifies a name change originally established by executive order in 2006.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The Maryland Port Administration (MPA) manages and operates the state-owned port facilities at the Helen Delich Bentley Port of Baltimore, and the bill codifies the port's official name across multiple sections of the Transportation Article governing the administration's operations.

MDOT is the parent department of the Maryland Port Administration and oversees state transportation facilities and freight routes, with the bill amending statutory references within the Transportation Article regarding access and port facilities.

The bill amends the Business Occupations and Professions Article regarding the membership qualifications of the State Board of Pilots, a professional licensing board housed within the Maryland Department of Labor.

qa_results.bill_summary: Requires the Prince George’s County Board of Education to hire an independent consultant to conduct a comprehensive feasibility study on relocating the Prince George’s County public school system headquarters before entering into a new long-term lease, and requires the consultant to report findings and recommendations by June 1, 2026.
qa_results.responsible_party: Prince George’s County Board of Education
qa_results.stakeholders: Prince George's County Public Schools, school staff, board members, students, parents, and county residents and businesses
qa_results.fiscal_impact_summary: Local expenditures for Prince George's County increase by an estimated $375,000 to cover the costs of the independent consultant's feasibility study. State operations are minimally affected, as the Maryland Stadium Authority can provide assistance using existing resources. Revenues are not affected.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill explicitly requires the independent consultant studying the feasibility of relocating the Prince George's County Public School System headquarters to engage with the Maryland Stadium Authority, which can provide assistance using existing resources.

qa_results.bill_summary: This bill alters the application and educational requirements for licensure as a dietitian-nutritionist under the State Board of Dietetic Practice, raising the minimum degree requirement to a master's degree as required by the Commission on Dietetic Registration, and updates statutory names of relevant certifying organizations.
qa_results.responsible_party: State Board of Dietetic Practice
qa_results.stakeholders: Applicants for dietitian-nutritionist licensure and practicing dietitian-nutritionists in Maryland.
qa_results.fiscal_impact_summary: The bill is technical in nature and has no state or local fiscal impact.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The State Board of Dietetic Practice is a health occupations licensing board operating under the Maryland Department of Health. The bill directly alters the licensing and application requirements that the Board administers and enforces.

qa_results.bill_summary: Prohibits a person from allowing certain animals—including bears, cougars, elephants, jaguars, leopards, lions, nonhuman primates, tigers, or their hybrids—to participate in traveling animal acts such as circuses or mobile exhibitions, with exceptions for fixed permanent facilities. Violations are subject to a civil penalty of up to $2,000.
qa_results.responsible_party: Department of Natural Resources, State or local law enforcement agencies, and local animal control authorities
qa_results.stakeholders: Traveling circuses, carnival operators, mobile animal exhibitors, wildlife performers, animal control agencies, and law enforcement
qa_results.fiscal_impact_summary: The bill is not anticipated to materially affect State or local operations or finances. Any enforcement by State and local law enforcement, the Department of Natural Resources, or local animal control authorities can be handled within existing budgeted resources.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill codifies prohibitions on traveling animal acts involving covered wildlife directly into the Natural Resources Article and explicitly authorizes officers and agents of the Department of Natural Resources (such as the Natural Resources Police) to enforce the provisions and issue civil penalties.
The bill authorizes State law enforcement officers, which includes the Maryland State Police, to enforce the prohibition on traveling animal acts featuring covered animals and issue civil citations.

qa_results.bill_summary: Prohibits the State Emergency Medical Services (EMS) Board from requiring applicants to provide proof of lawful presence in the United States or have a Social Security number (SSN) or Individual Taxpayer Identification Number (ITIN) as a condition for licensure or certification. Instead, applicants must provide an SSN, an ITIN, or allowable alternative documentation under federal law, which will be recorded and made available upon request to the Child Support Administration for enforcement purposes.
qa_results.responsible_party: State Emergency Medical Services Board (and the Maryland Institute for Emergency Medical Services Systems)
qa_results.stakeholders: Emergency medical service clinician applicants (including immigrants and individuals without a Social Security number or ITIN), licensed emergency health care clinicians, and the Child Support Administration within the Department of Human Services.
qa_results.fiscal_impact_summary: State implementation costs can be absorbed using existing budgeted resources. Special fund revenues for the Maryland Institute for Emergency Medical Services Systems (MIEMSS) may experience a minimal increase beginning in fiscal year 2025 if additional licensing fees are collected. The bill has no local government fiscal impact.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Maryland Institute for Emergency Medical Services Systems
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The State Emergency Medical Services (EMS) Board governs MIEMSS and is the primary entity impacted by the bill. The legislation prohibits the EMS Board from requiring proof of lawful presence or an SSN/ITIN as a condition of licensure or certification, adjusts application disclosure requirements, and directly affects MIEMSS's licensing administration and potential special fund fee revenues.

The bill amends the Family Law Article concerning occupational licensing and child support enforcement, requiring the EMS Board to collect and record applicant identification data (SSN, ITIN, or alternative documentation) to assist the Child Support Administration within DHS in collecting child support from obligors in arrears.

qa_results.bill_summary: Requires applicants for an initial optometry license or limited license, as well as currently licensed optometrists applying for their first license renewal on or after January 1, 2026, to submit to a state and national criminal history records check through the Criminal Justice Information System Central Repository.
qa_results.responsible_party: State Board of Examiners in Optometry
qa_results.stakeholders: Applicants for initial optometry licenses, applicants for limited optometry licenses, and licensed optometrists renewing their licenses on or after January 1, 2026.
qa_results.fiscal_impact_summary: State effect: Processing of criminal history records check results can be handled by the State Board of Examiners in Optometry with existing budgeted resources. Additional payments made by applicants ($51.25 per check) to the Criminal Justice Information System Central Repository are anticipated to cover the costs of conducting the checks. There is no local fiscal impact.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The State Board of Examiners in Optometry is a regulatory licensing board housed within the Maryland Department of Health. The bill requires the Board to mandate and review criminal history record checks for initial applicants and certain license renewals.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Department of Public Safety and Correctional Services
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill mandates that applicants apply to the Criminal Justice Information System Central Repository (CJIS-CR), a unit of DPSCS, to process State and national criminal history record checks and transmit results to the Board.

qa_results.bill_summary: Establishes exceptions to criminal trespass prohibitions and common law civil trespass liability for licensed professional land surveyors and their agents or employees who enter onto the property of another to practice land surveying.
qa_results.responsible_party: State Board for Professional Land Surveyors
qa_results.stakeholders: Professional land surveyors, their agents and employees, and real property owners in Maryland.
qa_results.fiscal_impact_summary: The bill is not expected to materially affect State or local government operations or finances.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The Maryland Department of Labor houses the State Board for Professional Land Surveyors, which licenses and regulates the professional land surveyors granted civil and criminal trespass exceptions under the bill.

The bill creates statutory exceptions to the common law civil tort of trespass and Title 6, Subtitle 4 criminal trespass offenses, directly affecting civil and criminal matters adjudicated in state courts.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Maryland Office of the Public Defender
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill creates an exception to criminal trespass charges, which directly affects criminal charges, defenses, and caseloads handled by public defenders representing indigent defendants.

As the primary state law enforcement agency enforcing state criminal statutes, MSP officers are affected when investigating and enforcing criminal trespass laws involving individuals engaged in land surveying.

qa_results.bill_summary: Enters Maryland into the interstate Cosmetology Licensure Compact, creating a multistate licensing framework that allows licensed cosmetologists to practice across member states. The bill establishes eligibility criteria, interstate data-sharing systems, disciplinary procedures, and governance under the Cosmetology Licensure Compact Commission, contingent upon adoption by at least six other states.
qa_results.responsible_party: State Board of Cosmetologists (Maryland Department of Labor)
qa_results.stakeholders: Licensed cosmetologists, cosmetology apprentices, relocating active-duty military members and their spouses, and consumers of cosmetology services in Maryland.
qa_results.fiscal_impact_summary: State special fund expenditures may increase to cover Maryland's share of costs for developing a coordinated multistate database and paying annual commission assessment fees, but the exact amount and timing are indeterminate. No material impact on special fund revenues is anticipated, as reductions in reciprocal license revenue are expected to be offset by multistate license fees. Local governments are not affected.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The Maryland Department of Labor houses the State Board of Cosmetologists, which serves as the State Licensing Authority responsible for administering the Cosmetology Licensure Compact, issuing multistate licenses, selecting the state's delegate to the Commission, submitting disciplinary data, and covering associated fees.
The bill formally enters Maryland into an interstate compact and establishes Maryland's membership in the Cosmetology Licensure Compact Commission.

qa_results.bill_summary: Requires Maryland employers to provide written notice of pay rates, regular paydays, and leave benefits at hire, and detailed written pay stubs or online pay statements for each pay period. Directs the Commissioner of Labor and Industry to offer a free pay stub template and establishes enforcement mechanisms and administrative penalties of up to $500 per employee for noncompliance.
qa_results.responsible_party: Commissioner of Labor and Industry (Maryland Department of Labor)
qa_results.stakeholders: Maryland private-sector employees and employers, including small business owners.
qa_results.fiscal_impact_summary: State implementation requirements can likely be absorbed within existing budgeted resources, and revenues are not materially affected. There is no local government fiscal impact because government entities are exempt as employers under the Wage Payment and Collection Law. Small businesses may incur administrative costs to update payroll reporting systems and could face penalties for noncompliance.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill directly tasks the Commissioner of Labor and Industry within the Maryland Department of Labor with creating and distributing a free pay stub template, investigating violations, issuing compliance orders and administrative penalties, and bringing enforcement actions.

Employers subject to an order or administrative penalty issued by the Commissioner of Labor and Industry have the right to request an administrative hearing conducted in accordance with the Administrative Procedure Act, which is adjudicated by the Office of Administrative Hearings.

The bill explicitly authorizes the Attorney General to bring a civil action against employers who fail to provide the required pay stub information, as well as provide legal representation to the Department of Labor in enforcement proceedings.

The bill creates a civil cause of action allowing employees and the Attorney General to file suit in the state court system, empowering courts to award injunctive relief, liquidated damages, and reasonable attorney's fees.

qa_results.bill_summary: Authorizes elementary schools participating in the Maryland Meals for Achievement In-Classroom Breakfast Program, with approval from the Maryland State Department of Education and the local school board, to serve breakfast in any broadly accessible part of the school—including from 'Grab and Go' carts—provided students may eat in the classroom after the school day starts. It also clarifies that participating secondary schools may serve breakfast in any broadly accessible part of the school.
qa_results.responsible_party: Maryland State Department of Education
qa_results.stakeholders: Elementary and secondary school students, participating public and eligible nonpublic schools, and local boards of education.
qa_results.fiscal_impact_summary: State Effect: None; the alterations are procedural and do not directly impact State finances. Local Effect: Participation flexibility may shift the number of breakfasts served and associated funding on a school-by-school basis, but statewide local participation remains constrained by the annual State appropriation.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The Maryland State Department of Education (MSDE) oversees and administers the Maryland Meals for Achievement (MMFA) Program and is specifically tasked with reviewing and approving applications from elementary schools to serve breakfast from broadly accessible areas, including grab-and-go carts.

qa_results.bill_summary: This bill amends the Public Information Act to allow employees or agents of the Baltimore City Department of Housing and Community Development (DHCD), rather than the Department of Public Works, to inspect surveillance images of illegal dumping. It also authorizes Baltimore City DHCD to publicly disseminate surveillance images of illegal dumping to the public as part of an investigation.
qa_results.responsible_party: Baltimore City Department of Housing and Community Development
qa_results.stakeholders: Individuals cited for or engaging in illegal dumping in Baltimore City, vehicle owners, Baltimore City residents, and Baltimore City code enforcement investigators.
qa_results.fiscal_impact_summary: State finances and operations are not materially affected. Baltimore City may see a minimal increase in fine revenues if the public release of images leads to identifying and convicting more violators. Local expenditures for litter removal may decrease if illegal dumping is deterred or if violators reimburse the city for cleanup costs. The provisions can be implemented with existing resources.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill amends the Maryland Public Information Act (PIA) regarding the confidentiality, inspection, and dissemination of surveillance images related to illegal dumping. The Office of the Attorney General serves as primary counsel regarding PIA compliance and statutory interpretation.

The District Court adjudicates citations and enforcement proceedings related to illegal dumping violations, though the bill focuses on municipal inspection and dissemination of surveillance images and is not expected to materially affect court caseloads or operations.

qa_results.bill_summary: This bill changes the statutory name of the Banneker-Douglass Museum, operated by the Commission on African American History and Culture in Annapolis, to the Banneker-Douglass-Tubman Museum.
qa_results.responsible_party: Maryland Commission on African American History and Culture
qa_results.stakeholders: Visitors to the museum, historians, cultural organizations, and members of the public interested in African American history and culture in Maryland.
qa_results.fiscal_impact_summary: State general fund expenditures increase by $10,100 in fiscal year 2025 only for one-time signage, printing, and creative support costs needed to rebrand the museum. State revenues and local finances are not affected.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Executive Commissions, Committees, Task Forces, and Advisory Boards
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill directly amends the statutory duties of the Commission on African American History and Culture, requiring the Commission to change the name of the museum it operates from the Banneker-Douglass Museum to the Banneker-Douglass-Tubman Museum, incurring one-time rebranding and signage costs.

The Department of Planning oversees the state's historical and cultural preservation programs and was consulted as an information source regarding the operational and facility impact of renaming the museum.

qa_results.bill_summary: Provides that a denial of a request for reconsideration of a finding of no probable cause by the Maryland Commission on Civil Rights is appealable in accordance with the Administrative Procedure Act, expanding appellate judicial review beyond the circuit court level.
qa_results.responsible_party: Maryland Commission on Civil Rights
qa_results.stakeholders: Complainants filing discrimination complaints with the Maryland Commission on Civil Rights, respondents to such complaints, and the state court system.
qa_results.fiscal_impact_summary: The bill is not anticipated to materially affect the operations or finances of the Maryland Commission on Civil Rights, the Judiciary, or local governments.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill directly governs the Maryland Commission on Civil Rights (MCCR) by specifying that a denial of a request for reconsideration of a finding of no probable cause by the Commission is a final order appealable under the Administrative Procedure Act.

The bill expands judicial review of MCCR no-probable-cause determinations, allowing appeals to proceed pursuant to the Administrative Procedure Act through the Circuit Court and the Appellate Court of Maryland.

The bill amends statutory appeal procedures to align with the Administrative Procedure Act, an administrative adjudication framework involving OAH and the courts, and OAH was consulted as an information source.

qa_results.bill_summary: This bill allows Prince George’s County to use proceeds from its local sales and use tax on energy and fuel to satisfy its education funding requirements under the state's maintenance of effort (MOE) and local share provisions, repealing the mandate that these revenues be appropriated to the school operating budget in addition to required local funding.
qa_results.responsible_party: Prince George's County Government
qa_results.stakeholders: Prince George's County Public Schools, students, school staff, and Prince George's County taxpayers.
qa_results.fiscal_impact_summary: State finances are not affected. Prince George's County expenditures for the county school system may decrease by $53.2 million in FY 2025 and up to $64.7 million in FY 2029 because energy and fuel tax revenues can now supplant rather than supplement required local appropriations. County revenues are unaffected.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill alters how Prince George's County satisfies its statutory local share and maintenance of effort (MOE) education funding requirements under § 5-235 of the Education Article, a framework overseen and administered statewide by the Maryland State Department of Education.

The Comptroller of Maryland serves as the state's chief tax administrator and financial officer, and was consulted regarding tax revenue and administration implications related to energy and fuel sales taxes.

qa_results.bill_summary: The Working for Accessible Renewable Maryland Thermal Heat (WARMTH) Act authorizes electric, gas, and water companies to own, manage, and recover costs for thermal energy network systems, subject to Public Service Commission (PSC) approval. It requires large gas companies serving at least 75,000 customers to submit pilot thermal energy network proposals to the PSC by July 1, 2025, with at least 80% of participating customers residing in low- or moderate-income housing. The Maryland Energy Administration (MEA) must coordinate funding sources, reserve $9 million in federal funding for behind-the-meter appliance installations, and provide grants of up to $1 million to community organizations for outreach.
qa_results.responsible_party: Public Service Commission and Maryland Energy Administration
qa_results.stakeholders: Gas and electric utility companies, residential utility ratepayers (especially low- and moderate-income households and overburdened communities), clean energy contractors, and community-based organizations.
qa_results.fiscal_impact_summary: State special fund expenditures for the PSC increase by $367,728 in FY 2025 and between $703,398 and $730,620 annually through FY 2029, offset by corresponding increases in special fund revenues assessed on public service companies. MEA special fund expenditures increase by $1,059,901 in FY 2025 (including $1.0 million for grants to community organizations) and by $103,594 to $117,872 annually through FY 2029. MEA must also reserve $9.0 million in federal funding for pilot project appliances. Transportation Trust Fund expenditures increase by $25,000 to $50,000 in FY 2025 for MDOT to perform a disparity study. Local government finances are not materially affected.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The Public Service Commission is the primary regulatory authority responsible for reviewing, approving, modifying, or rejecting pilot thermal energy network proposals, adopting decommissioning regulations, coordinating data collection, and overseeing utility cost recovery and rates.

MEA is tasked with coordinating major funding streams (including federal IRA, SEIF, and EmPOWER funds), reserving $9 million in federal funding for behind-the-meter appliance installations, awarding up to $1 million in community outreach grants, and consulting on the permanence of pilot systems.

OPC represents residential utility ratepayers in proceedings before the Commission, is statutorily required to be consulted by PSC when determining whether to make pilot systems permanent, and evaluates gas company pilot applications and associated rate impacts.
DHCD is required to coordinate with MEA to provide weatherization services and funding through EmPOWER programs for low- or moderate-income housing within the thermal energy network pilot areas.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Governor's Office of Small, Minority & Women Business Affairs
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: GOSBA is required, within six months of pilot system approval, to establish a plan setting reasonable and appropriate Minority Business Enterprise (MBE) participation goals and procedures in consultation with the Attorney General and participating utilities.

The Department of Labor's Commissioner of Labor and Industry determines prevailing wage rates applicable to projects under community benefit agreements, and the department is authorized to review and enforce compliance with these labor agreements and registered apprenticeship standards.
As the State's MBE certification agency, MDOT incurs expenditures from the Transportation Trust Fund to conduct an MBE disparity study necessary to support the bill's MBE provisions.
MES is statutorily referenced to comply with the State's Minority Business Enterprise program and submit annual reports on MBE participation for applicable thermal energy network projects.
The Office of the Attorney General is statutorily required to be consulted by GOSBA when establishing the plan for setting MBE participation goals and procedures for approved pilot systems.

qa_results.bill_summary: Authorizes the Prince George's County Council to impose an excise tax of up to $3.50 per month on each telephone line for telecommunications services, either in addition to or instead of the existing sales and use tax. It also allows the county to use the revenue generated from telecommunications taxes to satisfy its mandatory local education funding requirements (maintenance of effort and local share) rather than treating those funds as supplemental.
qa_results.responsible_party: Prince George's County Council
qa_results.stakeholders: Telecommunications customers and providers in Prince George's County, Prince George's County Public Schools, and the Prince George's County local government.
qa_results.fiscal_impact_summary: State effect: None. Local effect: Prince George's County revenues may increase by up to $48.3 million in FY 2025 and up to $49.3 million in FY 2029 if the maximum authorized excise tax is imposed. County local appropriation expenditures for the county school system may decrease by $13.1 million in FY 2025 and $16.0 million in FY 2029 because existing telecommunications tax proceeds can now be counted toward mandatory local funding requirements rather than being provided on top of them.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill allows Prince George's County to use revenues from its local telecommunications tax to satisfy local school funding requirements under § 5-235 of the Education Article (Maintenance of Effort and local share provisions), which the Maryland State Department of Education oversees and calculates for all local school systems.

As the state's chief tax administrator, the Comptroller monitors state sales and use tax policies and definitions cross-referenced in the bill (such as Tax - General Article Title 11 exemptions), although the tax authorized is collected locally by Prince George's County.

qa_results.bill_summary: Known as Gabriel's Law, the bill requires a law enforcement agency that receives a qualified request from an interested party to conduct an in-person wellness check without unreasonable delay, or forward the request to the appropriate jurisdiction if the individual is located elsewhere. If the request concerns a life-threatening condition, fire, rescue, or emergency medical services personnel must conduct the wellness check simultaneously with law enforcement.
qa_results.responsible_party: State and local law enforcement agencies and fire, rescue, or emergency medical services (EMS) entities
qa_results.stakeholders: Individuals requiring wellness checks for health or safety concerns, concerned family members and health care practitioners submitting requests, and first responders including police officers, firefighters, and EMS personnel
qa_results.fiscal_impact_summary: The bill is not expected to materially affect State or local revenues or expenditures, but it may have an operational impact on State and local law enforcement agencies and emergency medical services entities.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: As Maryland's primary statewide law enforcement agency, MSP is directly responsible for conducting in-person wellness checks without unreasonable delay upon receiving qualified requests, or forwarding such requests to the proper jurisdiction.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Maryland Institute for Emergency Medical Services Systems
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: MIEMSS oversees and coordinates the state's emergency medical services network. The bill requires EMS entities to conduct wellness checks simultaneously with law enforcement agencies when a qualified request indicates a life-threatening condition.
DNR operates the Natural Resources Police, a statewide law enforcement entity subject to the bill's operational mandates to respond to or transfer qualified wellness check requests.
MDTA maintains its own sworn police force, which is classified as a law enforcement agency and subject to the bill's requirements regarding wellness checks within its jurisdiction.
MDOT oversees several modal administrations with law enforcement personnel (such as MTA and MDTA police) that must comply with the requirements to conduct or refer qualified wellness checks.
USM institutions maintain sworn campus law enforcement agencies that must comply with the mandates to conduct wellness checks or refer requests to appropriate outside agencies.
Morgan State University operates its own campus police department, making it an affected law enforcement agency responsible for handling qualified wellness check requests.
St. Mary's College of Maryland maintains campus public safety and law enforcement officers who may receive and respond to qualified wellness check requests on campus.
DGS oversees the Maryland Capitol Police, a law enforcement agency that may be called upon to conduct or transfer qualified wellness checks in state-owned buildings and grounds.

qa_results.bill_summary: Adds an individual with experience in mental health care for veterans or individuals serving in the military to the list of categories from which a county governing body may appoint voting members to a county mental health advisory committee.
qa_results.responsible_party: County governing bodies
qa_results.stakeholders: County mental health advisory committees, veterans, military service members, and mental health providers specializing in veteran and military care.
qa_results.fiscal_impact_summary: No State or local fiscal impact. Modifying the potential membership categories for a county advisory committee does not affect government revenues or expenditures.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The Maryland Department of Health oversees public mental health and behavioral health policy and local core service agencies. The bill amends the Health - General Article governing county mental health advisory committees.

The bill adds an individual with experience in mental health care for veterans or active-duty military personnel to the categories of eligible appointees for county mental health advisory committees, directly touching the agency's mission to support veteran and military healthcare needs.

The Department of Aging is enumerated in the statute as one of the agencies from which representatives may be selected to serve on county mental health advisory committees, though this portion of the statute is not directly amended.

The Department of Juvenile Services is listed in the statute as an agency from which representatives may be appointed to county mental health advisory committees, though the bill does not amend its specific statutory provision.

qa_results.bill_summary: This bill alters the permissible uses of the Equitech Growth Fund within the Maryland Technology Development Corporation (TEDCO) to allow fund proceeds to be used for the payment of administrative costs in addition to making program awards. It also adjusts the existing $5.0 million annual mandated appropriation for fiscal years 2025 through 2033 so that funds are appropriated directly to the Fund rather than solely for awards.
qa_results.responsible_party: Maryland Technology Development Corporation (TEDCO)
qa_results.stakeholders: Public, nonprofit, and private entities in Maryland (including higher education institutions and small businesses) seeking Equitech Growth Fund awards, workforce participants in emerging and advanced industries, and TEDCO.
qa_results.fiscal_impact_summary: State General Fund expenditures for TEDCO decrease by $600,000 annually beginning in FY 2025, as administrative expenses are absorbed by the existing $5.0 million mandated appropriation rather than requiring additional general funds. Special fund revenues and expenditures decrease correspondingly by $600,000 annually. Because funds available for awards decrease to cover administrative costs, awards to higher education institutions, local governments, and small businesses may decrease beginning in FY 2025.
