agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill directly governs the Department of Natural Resources' authority to manage oyster fisheries and alter or reduce the boundaries of established oyster sanctuaries, while maintaining requirements for the scientific oyster fishery management plan.

The statute specifically references collaboration and consultation with the University of Maryland Center for Environmental Science (a USM institution) regarding the scientific modeling tool and consensus recommendations for oyster stock management.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Executive Commissions, Committees, Task Forces, and Advisory Boards
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The Oyster Advisory Commission is statutorily tasked within the bill's provisions with reviewing model results and developing consensus recommendations to inform oyster fishery management actions.

qa_results.bill_summary: Extends the expiration dates of two specific Class B-D-7 alcoholic beverages licenses in Baltimore City (in the 5517 block of Harford Road and the 2200 block of East Fayette Street) until July 1, 2025, to allow license transfers and renewals, contingent upon entering into memorandums of understanding with designated community associations.
qa_results.responsible_party: Baltimore City Board of License Commissioners
qa_results.stakeholders: Alcoholic beverages license holders and applicants in the 5517 block of Harford Road and the 2200 block of East Fayette Street, the Hamilton Community Association, the C.A.R.E. Community Association, and local Baltimore City residents.
qa_results.fiscal_impact_summary: State finances are not affected. Baltimore City revenues may increase minimally in FY 2025 from applicable license renewal and transfer fees (annual Class B-D-7 fee is $1,320 and renewal fee is $50).

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill concerns the extension and transfer conditions of specific retail alcoholic beverage licenses in Baltimore City. While these local licenses are administered directly by the Baltimore City Board of License Commissioners with no state fiscal impact, the Comptroller of Maryland oversees state-level regulation and taxation of the alcohol industry.

qa_results.bill_summary: This bill establishes a revised process for academic program approval and institutional mission statement evaluations overseen by the Maryland Higher Education Commission (MHEC), based on State and regional workforce needs. It mandates collaboration among MHEC, the Maryland Department of Labor, and the Department of Commerce to establish baseline workforce data; creates a Program Review Process Advisory Council; establishes the Proposed Programs Collaborative Grant Fund to incentivize institutional partnerships on new graduate programs; provides specific lead times for historically Black colleges and universities (HBCUs) and the University of Maryland, College Park to propose emerging workforce need graduate programs; and sets up distinct review processes for online programs and periodic reviews of programs previously approved over HBCU objections.
qa_results.responsible_party: Maryland Higher Education Commission (MHEC), in coordination with the Maryland Department of Labor and the Department of Commerce
qa_results.stakeholders: Maryland public and private postsecondary institutions (including HBCUs, public universities, private nonprofit colleges, and community colleges), postsecondary faculty and students, and Maryland employers and workforce segments.
qa_results.fiscal_impact_summary: State general fund expenditures increase by at least $264,000 in FY 2025 (reflecting $164,039 for two researcher positions across MHEC and MDL and at least $100,000 for one-time system data integration costs at the Maryland Longitudinal Data System Center), with ongoing general fund costs ranging between $195,900 and $222,900 annually through FY 2029. Revenues and expenditures for public higher education institutions and local community colleges may shift under the new program approval and collaboration processes. Additional special fund revenues and expenditures could occur if the Proposed Programs Collaborative Grant Fund receives an appropriation, potentially exceeding $250,000 annually.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: MHEC is the primary implementing agency responsible for updating the State Plan for Higher Education, overhauling academic program approval processes, reviewing institutional mission statements, establishing the Program Review Process Advisory Council, and administering the Proposed Programs Collaborative Grant Fund.

As the primary state higher education coordinating agency, the commission is charged with executing extensive new duties under the bill, including program review, workforce data integration, and administering collaborative grants.

The bill mandates that the Department of Labor maintain a dedicated full-time staff member to compile state and regional workforce data collaboratively with MHEC and Commerce to inform postsecondary education policies, resulting in direct fiscal and operational impacts.
The bill statutorily requires the Department of Commerce to define, compile, and coordinate baseline workforce data alongside MHEC and the Department of Labor to inform higher education policy.

USM and its constituent institutions (including HBCUs and UMCP) are directly subject to revised academic program approval procedures, letter of intent requirements, mission statement reviews, and priority windows for emerging workforce need programs.

Morgan State University is explicitly granted priority lead status to propose graduate-level emerging workforce need programs, is protected under HBCU program duplication objection reviews, and must comply with new program submission requirements.

As a public senior higher education institution, SMCM must comply with updated academic program approval rules, mandatory bi-annual letters of intent for graduate programs, and institutional mission statement reviews.

The bill specifies consultation with the MLDS Center to identify workforce needs data, incurring estimated one-time general fund costs of $100,000 to $200,000 to incorporate workforce needs and projections into its database.

The bill requires MHEC to consult with the Attorney General to adopt regulations setting standards for analyzing objections based on unnecessary program duplication under state and federal equal educational opportunity obligations.
The State Treasurer is required to hold and invest monies in the newly established Proposed Programs Collaborative Grant Fund.
The Comptroller is statutorily designated to account for the newly established Proposed Programs Collaborative Grant Fund.

qa_results.bill_summary: The Distributed Renewable Integration and Vehicle Electrification (DRIVE) Act requires investor-owned electric companies to file opt-in time-of-use tariffs with enrollment targets and to submit pilot programs or temporary tariffs to compensate distributed energy resource owners and aggregators for electric distribution system support services. Additionally, it directs the Public Service Commission to establish expedited interconnection regulations for bidirectional electric vehicle systems and authorizes utility cost recovery and incentives for customer-sited renewable generation and storage.
qa_results.responsible_party: Public Service Commission
qa_results.stakeholders: Investor-owned electric companies, municipal electric utilities and electric cooperatives, electricity customers (including low- and moderate-income households), and owners and aggregators of distributed energy resources, energy storage, and bidirectional electric vehicles.
qa_results.fiscal_impact_summary: Public Service Commission special fund expenditures increase by $410,628 in FY 2025 (including two new positions and $250,000 in consultant costs), $441,700 in FY 2026, $450,000 in FY 2027, $458,500 in FY 2028, and $217,400 in FY 2029. Special fund revenues increase correspondingly via assessments on public service companies. Office of People's Counsel special fund expenditures and revenues may also increase beginning in FY 2025. Local government finances are not materially affected.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The Public Service Commission is the primary implementing agency responsible for approving time-of-use tariffs, adopting regulations for bidirectional electric vehicle interconnection, developing the electric distribution system support services pilot program, and overseeing utility cost recovery and incentives.

The Office of the People's Counsel is directly impacted as the state's residential utility consumer advocate, requiring participation in extensive PSC regulatory and tariff proceedings associated with time-of-use rates and distributed energy resource pilot programs.

The Maryland Energy Administration is statutorily required to consult with the Public Service Commission to ensure that utility incentives or rebates for renewable on-site generating systems effectively supplement other state and federal incentives.

qa_results.bill_summary: This bill expands health insurance coverage requirements by adding image-guided breast biopsy to the definition of supplemental breast examinations, thereby exempting it from cost-sharing requirements such as copayments, coinsurance, and deductibles (except for high-deductible health plans). It also clarifies that mandated coverage for lung cancer screening encompasses follow-up diagnostic imaging and prohibits insurers, health service plans, and health maintenance organizations from requiring prior authorization for lung cancer screening or follow-up diagnostic imaging.
qa_results.responsible_party: Maryland Insurance Administration
qa_results.stakeholders: Individuals requiring breast or lung cancer screenings and follow-up imaging or biopsies, health insurance carriers, nonprofit health service plans, and health maintenance organizations.
qa_results.fiscal_impact_summary: State special fund revenues for the Maryland Insurance Administration will see a minimal increase in FY 2025 from the $125 rate and form filing fee, with form reviews handled within existing budgeted resources. There is no impact on the State Employee and Retiree Health and Welfare Benefits Program as it already complies. Local government expenditures may see a potential minimal increase for jurisdictions purchasing fully insured health plans if insurance premiums rise.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: As the primary regulator of commercial health insurance carriers and HMOs in Maryland, the Maryland Insurance Administration is responsible for enforcing the coverage and prior authorization requirements and reviewing policy form and rate filings submitted by insurers.
DBM oversees the State Employee and Retiree Health and Welfare Benefits Program, which must monitor and maintain compliance with statutory health insurance benefit mandates.
MHBE administers the state health benefit marketplace and ensures that qualified health plans sold to individuals and small employers comply with state-mandated health benefit requirements.

qa_results.bill_summary: This bill requires the Maryland Department of the Environment (MDE), upon request, to permit nonuniform payment schedules in Clean Water Commerce Account contracts for projects involving construction, reconstruction, or rehabilitation. Under these contracts, the cost-per-pound of nitrogen reduced may vary upon reaching agreed performance milestones, provided the first milestone occurs after construction or rehabilitation is complete. The bill also authorizes MDE to require a minimum final payment and, for contracts over $500,000, additional financial protections such as performance bonds, insurance, or letters of credit.
qa_results.responsible_party: Maryland Department of the Environment
qa_results.stakeholders: Project owners, contractors, small businesses, and local governments that enter into contracts under the Clean Water Commerce Account for environmental outcome projects.
qa_results.fiscal_impact_summary: State special fund administrative expenditures from the Bay Restoration Fund increase by an unknown but likely modest amount starting in FY 2025 due to added complexity in administering nonuniform payment schedules. The bill does not change the overall funding of the Clean Water Commerce Account ($20 million transferred annually from the Bay Restoration Fund through FY 2030). Local government finances may be significantly affected as potential recipients of CWCA contract funding depending on contract structuring and proposal competitiveness.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill directly amends the contracting requirements of the Clean Water Commerce Account administered by the Maryland Department of the Environment (MDE). It requires MDE to allow nonuniform payment schedules for certain environmental outcome contracts and authorizes MDE to require minimum final payments or additional financial protections (e.g., letters of credit or performance bonds). MDE also incurs modest additional special fund administrative expenditures to implement the bill.

qa_results.bill_summary: Authorizes the Baltimore County Board of License Commissioners to satisfy the public notice requirement for alcoholic beverages license application hearings by posting the notice online at least 14 days before the hearing date, rather than publishing it in a local newspaper of general circulation.
qa_results.responsible_party: Baltimore County Board of License Commissioners
qa_results.stakeholders: Alcoholic beverage license applicants, Baltimore County residents, local newspapers in Baltimore County, and the Baltimore County government.
qa_results.fiscal_impact_summary: State effect: None. Local effect: Baltimore County expenditures decrease by as much as approximately $40,000 annually beginning in fiscal year 2025 due to reduced advertising costs from publishing notices online rather than in local newspapers. Local revenues are unaffected.

qa_results.bill_summary: This bill updates vehicle laws to clarify that motor vehicle manufacturers, distributors, and factory branches may not refuse to deliver new vehicles or truck component parts to licensed dealers or distributors after receiving an electronic order, under specified conditions and within a reasonable timeframe.
qa_results.responsible_party: Maryland Department of Transportation
qa_results.stakeholders: Motor vehicle manufacturers, distributors, factory branches, and licensed motor vehicle dealers
qa_results.fiscal_impact_summary: The bill does not affect State finances or operations, and has no local government effect. Any impact on small businesses is minimal.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The Motor Vehicle Administration regulates vehicle dealers, manufacturers, and distributors under Title 15 of the Transportation Article, which governs business licensing and commercial delivery requirements amended by the bill.

The Department of Transportation oversees the Motor Vehicle Administration and administers the state's Transportation Article, within which the manufacturer and dealer delivery provisions are enacted.

qa_results.bill_summary: Authorizes Baltimore City, counties, and municipalities to establish designated tourism zones and offer tax incentives to qualifying tourism enterprises within those zones, including exemptions from local admissions and amusement taxes and property tax credits on qualifying real and personal property.
qa_results.responsible_party: Comptroller of Maryland
qa_results.stakeholders: Local governments, qualifying for-profit and nonprofit tourism enterprises, small businesses located in tourism zones, and consumers of tourism and amusement activities.
qa_results.fiscal_impact_summary: State finances are not affected. Local property tax and admissions and amusement tax revenues may decrease beginning in fiscal 2025 to the extent local jurisdictions designate tourism zones and grant tax credits and exemptions. Baltimore City estimates its local revenues could decrease by approximately $6.4 million annually if credits and exemptions are implemented there. Local expenditures are not affected.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill explicitly requires political subdivisions establishing a tourism zone to notify the Comptroller prior to establishment, and report any qualifying tourism enterprises eligible for admissions and amusement tax exemptions, including effective and expiration dates.

The Department of Commerce oversees statewide economic development, tourism policy, and the Arts and Entertainment District program referenced in the legislation, which coordinates with the newly authorized tourism zones.

As the state agency responsible for driving tourism-related economic development and promoting visitor destinations across Maryland, the office's core mission aligns closely with the establishment and promotion of local tourism zones.

qa_results.bill_summary: House Bill 1287 consolidates two existing school leadership training programs into a single, unified program developed by the Maryland State Department of Education and the Accountability and Implementation Board. It mandates completion of the program at least once for the State Superintendent, local school superintendents, and the chairs and vice chairs of the State Board of Education, local school boards, and the Accountability and Implementation Board, while encouraging attendance for other board members, senior instructional staff, and principals. Additionally, it adjusts the program duration to 12 months, incorporates both virtual and in-person formats, and updates the curriculum to include topics such as attracting and retaining a diverse and inclusive educator workforce.
qa_results.responsible_party: Maryland State Department of Education and the Accountability and Implementation Board
qa_results.stakeholders: State Superintendent of Schools, county superintendents, chairs and vice chairs of the State Board of Education, local boards of education, and the Accountability and Implementation Board, as well as senior instruction-related staff and school principals.
qa_results.fiscal_impact_summary: State expenditures are not expected to increase beyond existing requirements, as MSDE and AIB can adapt the single leadership training program using existing resources. Minimal attendance cost savings may be realized for the State Board of Education, while minimal additional costs may be incurred by AIB. Local school systems can facilitate required training participation using existing resources, with potential minimal savings from virtual offerings and a shorter program duration. Neither state nor local revenues are affected.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill directly tasks the Maryland State Department of Education (MSDE) with collaborating to establish a unified school leadership training program and requires the State Superintendent of Schools and leadership of the State Board of Education to complete the program.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Executive Commissions, Committees, Task Forces, and Advisory Boards
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The Accountability and Implementation Board (AIB), an independent state body, is co-tasked with developing the school leadership training program, and its chair, vice chair, and members are directly required or encouraged to complete the training.

qa_results.bill_summary: Requires the Maryland Department of Health to develop and implement a three-year public education campaign on prostate, lung, and breast cancer prevention, focusing on communities disproportionately impacted by these cancers.
qa_results.responsible_party: Maryland Department of Health
qa_results.stakeholders: Communities disproportionately impacted by prostate, lung, and breast cancer, as well as healthcare providers, hospitals, and health organizations.
qa_results.fiscal_impact_summary: State Cigarette Restitution Fund (CRF) expenditures are not materially affected overall, but up to $750,000 in total CRF funding will shift from existing programs to the public education campaign across fiscal years 2026 through 2030 (capped at $750,000 total). If CRF funds are reallocated away from Medicaid, up to $750,000 in general fund expenditures may be required to backfill Medicaid. Revenues are not affected, and there is no direct impact on local governments.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: MDH is the primary agency tasked with developing, implementing, and setting measurable goals for the three-year public education campaign on prostate, lung, and breast cancer prevention, as well as reporting on its outcomes.

The bill mandates that the Governor include an appropriation from the Cigarette Restitution Fund of up to $750,000 total across fiscal years 2026 through 2030 in the annual budget bill for the public education campaign.
DBM oversees the development and execution of the state budget, which is impacted by the mandated budget appropriation from the Cigarette Restitution Fund and potential shifting of funding.

qa_results.bill_summary: House Bill 1296 alters regulations and procurement processes for Maryland offshore wind projects. It requires the Public Service Commission (PSC) to open an expedited proceeding to evaluate revised schedules, capacity, or pricing for previously approved Round 2 offshore wind projects and permits Round 1 projects to seek amendments to increase their offshore wind renewable energy credit (OREC) sales. It also directs the PSC and partner agencies to create a plan to reach 8,500 megawatts of offshore wind capacity by 2031, removes the 5.0 million megawatt-hour annual cap on offshore wind procurement by the Department of General Services (DGS), and mandates a second procurement solicitation.
qa_results.responsible_party: Public Service Commission and the Department of General Services
qa_results.stakeholders: Offshore wind energy developers, electric utility ratepayers, renewable energy labor organizations and contractors, and State agencies purchasing electricity.
qa_results.fiscal_impact_summary: General fund expenditures for DGS increase by $400,000 across FY 2025 and FY 2026 for consultant costs to administer a second procurement and help develop the capacity plan. DNR general/special fund expenditures may increase by up to $350,000 in FY 2025 for consultant support. PSC can likely manage reviews with existing resources, though minimal special fund expenditures and matching assessment revenues may occur. Future State electricity expenditures under modified long-term power purchase agreements are unknown but potentially significant beginning around FY 2026. Local government finances are not directly affected.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill directly requires the Public Service Commission to open proceedings evaluating revised Round 2 offshore wind projects, review Round 1 order amendment requests regarding ORECs, and develop a comprehensive plan to reach 8,500 MW of offshore wind capacity by 2031.

The bill modifies the Department of General Services' offshore wind energy procurement responsibilities, requiring DGS to issue solicitations and draft solicitations for power purchase agreements without the previous 5,000,000 MWh cap, requiring a second procurement, and incurring an estimated $400,000 in general fund expenditures for consultant costs.

The bill grants MEA access to confidential information relating to the revised Round 2 offshore wind proceedings and requires MEA to assist the Public Service Commission in developing the 8,500 MW offshore wind energy capacity plan.

The bill tasks the Department of Natural Resources with assisting the Public Service Commission in developing the offshore wind capacity plan, which the fiscal note indicates may increase DNR expenditures by up to $350,000 in FY 2025 for consultant costs.
The bill specifically directs the Department of the Environment to assist the Public Service Commission in developing the plan for achieving 8,500 megawatts of offshore wind energy capacity by 2031.

As the advocate for residential utility customers in Public Service Commission proceedings, OPC is directly affected by the revised Round 2 and Round 1 offshore wind proceedings and their associated ratepayer impact and pricing determinations.

qa_results.bill_summary: This bill updates and expands the statutory definition of "provide esthetic services" to include specific procedures such as cosmetic microneedling, superficial exfoliation, eyelash extensions, and nonablative skin rejuvenation. It also explicitly specifies that esthetic services do not include the diagnosis of illness, disease, or injury, or performing ablation of the dermis or hypodermis.
qa_results.responsible_party: State Board of Cosmetologists within the Maryland Department of Labor
qa_results.stakeholders: Licensed cosmetologists, estheticians, salon and spa small businesses, and clients receiving esthetic skin and beauty services
qa_results.fiscal_impact_summary: The bill is not anticipated to materially affect the State Board of Cosmetologists' finances or operations, and the board can implement the changes with existing resources. There is no local government fiscal impact. Small businesses may experience a meaningful economic benefit through the ability to offer and charge for an expanded range of authorized esthetic services.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill alters the scope of practice and statutory definition of 'provide esthetic services,' which directly affects licensees regulated by the State Board of Cosmetologists housed within the Maryland Department of Labor.

qa_results.bill_summary: Requires the Maryland Department of Health to establish a process for providing information on the State's earned income tax credit to enrollees and potential enrollees in specified health, prescription, and long-term care programs. It also requires the Maryland Department of Aging to provide periodic training to the Maryland Access Point network to raise awareness of the tax credit.
qa_results.responsible_party: Maryland Department of Health and Maryland Department of Aging
qa_results.stakeholders: Enrollees and prospective enrollees in Maryland Medical Assistance, Maryland Children's Health Program, Qualified State Long-Term Care Insurance Partnership, Senior Prescription Drug Assistance Program, and Prescription Drug Repository Program, as well as low- to moderate-income taxpayers and the Maryland Access Point network.
qa_results.fiscal_impact_summary: State agencies can implement the bill with existing budgeted resources. State general fund revenues and local revenues may decrease beginning in FY 2025 to the extent the bill leads to increased claims of the State and local earned income and poverty level tax credits (impact is indeterminate). Montgomery County expenditures for its Working Families Income Supplement Program may also increase beginning in FY 2025.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: HB 1304 directly mandates the Maryland Department of Health to develop a process for providing information regarding the availability of the State's Earned Income Tax Credit (EITC) to enrollees, potential enrollees, and service recipients across multiple programs, including Medical Assistance, MCHP, Long-Term Care Insurance Partnership, and prescription drug assistance programs.

The bill explicitly requires the Maryland Department of Aging to provide periodic training to the Maryland Access Point network to increase awareness of the availability of the State's Earned Income Tax Credit.

As the state's tax collector administering the Earned Income Tax Credit, the Comptroller is impacted by the bill, which aims to increase taxpayer awareness and utilization of the EITC, thereby potentially decreasing general fund tax revenues.

The fiscal note highlights that the Qualified State Long-Term Care Insurance Partnership is jointly administered by the Department of Health and the Maryland Insurance Administration, noting that MDH may require MIA's assistance in distributing EITC information to policyholders.

Originally included in the bill's distribution mandates before being amended out, DHS is a statutory partner cooperating with the Department of Aging on the Maryland Access Point program and served as an information source for the fiscal analysis.

qa_results.bill_summary: This bill prohibits a person from recording a deed or other instrument knowing that it contains false information, such as ownership details. Violations are classified as a misdemeanor punishable by a fine of up to $500, with a three-year statute of limitations for prosecution. Additionally, it authorizes courts to award costs and reasonable attorney's fees to either party in an action to quiet title if a claim or defense involves an alleged recordation of a false instrument.
qa_results.responsible_party: Maryland Judiciary (District Court and Circuit Courts) and local clerks of the court
qa_results.stakeholders: Property owners, buyers and sellers of real property, litigants and attorneys involved in quiet title actions, and individuals recording deeds or land records.
qa_results.fiscal_impact_summary: State and local government operations and finances are not anticipated to be materially affected. Fine revenues collected from misdemeanor cases in the District Court may increase minimally.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: HB 1308 directly impacts the Maryland court system by creating a new misdemeanor offense for recording instruments with false information (prosecuted in the District Court), extending the statute of limitations to three years, and granting courts statutory authority to award costs and reasonable attorney's fees in quiet title actions involving such violations.

qa_results.bill_summary: Authorizes a Southern Maryland code county to include in its subdivision regulations provisions for the dedication of real property for recreation, or the payment of a fee in lieu of dedication to be used for the purchase, development, and improvement of recreational facilities.
qa_results.responsible_party: Southern Maryland code county governments (specifically Charles County, as the only currently eligible code county)
qa_results.stakeholders: Land developers, small business developers, and residents of Southern Maryland code counties (primarily Charles County).
qa_results.fiscal_impact_summary: State finances are not materially affected. Charles County revenues and expenditures may increase to the extent the county exercises this authority to collect in-lieu fees and fund recreational facilities, though it is unclear how much this authority expands upon existing development impact fee authority.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill amends the Land Use Article concerning local subdivision regulations and property dedication for recreational facilities in Southern Maryland code counties. The Department of Planning provides policy guidance and technical assistance to local governments on comprehensive land use and subdivision planning.

qa_results.bill_summary: This bill allows individuals monitored by a private home detention monitoring agency as a condition of probation to earn compliance credits to reduce their term of home detention. It also requires private home detention monitoring agencies to submit compliance reports to the Division of Parole and Probation upon request.
qa_results.responsible_party: Division of Parole and Probation (Department of Public Safety and Correctional Services)
qa_results.stakeholders: Individuals on probation subject to private home detention monitoring, private home detention monitoring agencies, and the Judiciary.
qa_results.fiscal_impact_summary: State finances are not materially affected, though the Judiciary may experience a minimal, absorbable expenditure increase to handle adjustments to home detention periods. State revenues are unaffected. Local government operations and finances are not materially affected. Small business private home detention monitoring agencies may experience a meaningful fiscal impact resulting from reduced monitoring durations.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Department of Public Safety and Correctional Services
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill directly tasks the Department and its Division of Parole and Probation with expanding the earned compliance credit and abatement program to individuals monitored by private home detention monitoring agencies, receiving compliance reports from these agencies, and tracking credits.

The Judiciary is required to adjust periods of home detention and probation upon recommendation by the Division of Parole and Probation, as well as handle proceedings if an individual violates probation while on abatement.

qa_results.bill_summary: Lowers the minimum age from 18 to 16 for an individual who may be employed by an alcoholic beverages licensee in Allegany County, while maintaining the requirement that an employee must be at least 18 years old to sell or serve alcoholic beverages.
qa_results.responsible_party: Allegany County Board of License Commissioners
qa_results.stakeholders: Alcoholic beverage licensees and 16- and 17-year-old job seekers in Allegany County.
qa_results.fiscal_impact_summary: The bill has no effect on State finances and does not materially affect Allegany County operations or finances. Any effect on small businesses is minimal.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill alters the minimum legal age for employment by alcoholic beverage license holders in Allegany County to allow individuals aged 16 and 17 to be employed (provided they do not sell or serve alcohol). The Maryland Department of Labor oversees and enforces state labor and employment standards, including youth employment regulations.
The Comptroller of Maryland regulates the state's alcohol industry, although local licensing boards handle local operational rules and enforcement.

qa_results.bill_summary: This bill alters the membership, leadership, purpose, and duties of the Maryland Commission on Health Equity (MCHE), directing it to develop and monitor a statewide health equity plan under federal Center for Medicare and Medicaid Innovation agreements. It also designates the Secretary of Health and the Executive Director of the Health Services Cost Review Commission as cochairs of MCHE, alters reporting requirements for the Commission on Public Health, and extends the termination date of the Commission on Public Health by one year to June 30, 2026.
qa_results.responsible_party: Maryland Department of Health, Health Services Cost Review Commission, and Maryland Commission on Health Equity
qa_results.stakeholders: Maryland residents (particularly underserved and minority communities), health care facilities, hospitals, clinicians and providers, health insurers, managed care organizations, and public health agencies
qa_results.fiscal_impact_summary: State revenues are unaffected. Additional workload and expense reimbursements for the Maryland Department of Health, Health Services Cost Review Commission, and Maryland Commission on Health Equity, as well as costs associated with extending the Commission on Public Health's termination date, can be absorbed within existing budgeted resources. Local governments are not fiscally affected.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill designates the Secretary of Health (or designee) as cochair of the Maryland Commission on Health Equity, requires the department to provide staff support, includes multiple deputy secretaries as members, and tasks the department with coordinating on advisory committees and implementing the statewide health equity plan.

The Executive Director of the HSCRC is designated to cochair the Maryland Commission on Health Equity, advise on member appointments, and collaborate on the advisory committee and statewide health equity plan required under federal CMMI agreements.

The Executive Director of the Maryland Health Care Commission is added as a statutory member of the Maryland Commission on Health Equity, and data from health care payers reporting to MHCC is incorporated into the commission's health equity data set.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Executive Commissions, Committees, Task Forces, and Advisory Boards
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill directly reorganizes the Maryland Commission on Health Equity and alters reporting dates and extends the termination date of the Commission on Public Health.
The Maryland Insurance Commissioner continues to serve as a designated member of the Maryland Commission on Health Equity.
The Secretary of Aging (or designee) continues to serve as a statutory member of the Maryland Commission on Health Equity.
The Secretary of Budget and Management (or designee) continues to serve as a member of the Maryland Commission on Health Equity.
The Secretary of Disabilities (or designee) continues to serve as a statutory member of the Maryland Commission on Health Equity.
The State Superintendent of Schools (or designee) continues to serve as a member of the Maryland Commission on Health Equity.
The Secretary of Housing and Community Development (or designee) continues to serve on the Maryland Commission on Health Equity.
The Secretary of Human Services (or designee) continues to serve as a member of the Maryland Commission on Health Equity.
The Secretary of Planning (or designee) continues to serve as a member of the Maryland Commission on Health Equity.

The bill removes the Governor's authority to designate the chair of the Maryland Commission on Health Equity and alters the reporting schedule for reports submitted to the Governor by the Commission on Public Health.
The bill removes the Secretary of Agriculture from statutory membership on the Maryland Commission on Health Equity.
The bill removes the Secretary of Commerce from statutory membership on the Maryland Commission on Health Equity.
The bill removes the Secretary of General Services from statutory membership on the Maryland Commission on Health Equity.
The bill removes the Secretary of Information Technology from statutory membership on the Maryland Commission on Health Equity.
The bill removes the Secretary of Juvenile Services from statutory membership on the Maryland Commission on Health Equity.
The bill removes the Secretary of Labor from statutory membership on the Maryland Commission on Health Equity.
The bill removes the Secretary of Natural Resources from statutory membership on the Maryland Commission on Health Equity.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Department of Public Safety and Correctional Services
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill removes the Commissioner of Correction from statutory membership on the Maryland Commission on Health Equity.
The bill removes the Secretary of Transportation from statutory membership on the Maryland Commission on Health Equity.
The bill removes the Secretary of Veterans Affairs from statutory membership on the Maryland Commission on Health Equity.
The bill removes the Secretary of the Environment from statutory membership on the Maryland Commission on Health Equity.
The bill removes the Secretary of State Police from statutory membership on the Maryland Commission on Health Equity.

qa_results.bill_summary: This bill permanently extends the Continuing the CORE Partnership Fund within the Department of Housing and Community Development by repealing its termination date, and mandates that the Governor include an annual appropriation of $50,000,000 for the fund in the State operating budget beginning in fiscal year 2026 to assist in the removal of blighted property in Baltimore City.
qa_results.responsible_party: Department of Housing and Community Development
qa_results.stakeholders: Residents and neighborhoods of Baltimore City affected by vacant and blighted properties, the Baltimore City local government, and the Maryland Stadium Authority.
qa_results.fiscal_impact_summary: Beginning in FY 2026, State pay-as-you-go (PAYGO) general fund expenditures increase by $50.0 million annually due to the mandated appropriation. To the extent PAYGO funds replace general obligation (GO) bonds planned for Project CORE in the Capital Improvement Program, those bonds will be freed up for other capital projects. The bill has no fiscal effect in FY 2024 or FY 2025, and is not expected to materially affect Baltimore City finances unless the mandated funding supplements rather than replaces planned capital spending.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: DHCD is the primary agency responsible for administering the Continuing the CORE Partnership Fund and overseeing Project CORE demolition and revitalization efforts in Baltimore City.
MSA is explicitly named in the statute as a key partner working in conjunction with DHCD and Baltimore City to expeditiously remove blighted property under Project CORE.
The bill mandates the Governor to include an annual appropriation of $50,000,000 to the Fund in the state budget bill beginning in fiscal year 2026.
DBM prepares the state budget and must incorporate and execute the bill's $50,000,000 annual mandated PAYGO general fund appropriation starting in fiscal year 2026.
The State Treasurer is statutorily designated to hold the Continuing the CORE Partnership Fund separately and invest its moneys in the same manner as other state funds.
The Comptroller is statutorily required to account for the Continuing the CORE Partnership Fund.

qa_results.bill_summary: Expands quarterly reporting requirements for health insurance carriers by requiring them to report to the Maryland Insurance Commissioner the number of members entitled to health care benefits in the State and the number of clean claims processed for reimbursement.
qa_results.responsible_party: Maryland Insurance Commissioner (Maryland Insurance Administration)
qa_results.stakeholders: Health insurance carriers operating in Maryland and health insurance policyholders and consumers
qa_results.fiscal_impact_summary: The bill does not substantively change State activities or operations. There is no local fiscal impact or small business effect.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: HB 1337 directly impacts the Maryland Insurance Administration, headed by the Insurance Commissioner. The bill alters carrier reporting requirements by mandating quarterly reporting on member totals and processed clean claims, which the Commissioner must collect and incorporate into an annual summary report.
The bill requires the Maryland Insurance Commissioner to submit copies of the annual summary report on health insurance appeals and grievances to the Governor.

qa_results.bill_summary: Decreases the term of office from five years to three years for members of the agricultural preservation advisory board in Howard County, while permitting current members to finish out their existing five-year terms.
qa_results.responsible_party: Howard County Government
qa_results.stakeholders: Members of the Howard County Agricultural Preservation Advisory Board and agricultural landowners in Howard County.
qa_results.fiscal_impact_summary: The bill has no state fiscal impact and does not materially affect Howard County operations or finances.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill amends the Maryland Agriculture Code regarding local agricultural preservation advisory boards, which directly interface with and advise the Maryland Agricultural Land Preservation Foundation (MALPF) housed within the Maryland Department of Agriculture.

qa_results.bill_summary: Requires health insurers, nonprofit health service plans, and health maintenance organizations to provide coverage for medically necessary hearing aids for adults when prescribed, fitted, and dispensed by a licensed audiologist, while permitting carriers to limit coverage to $1,400 per ear every 36 months.
qa_results.responsible_party: Maryland Insurance Administration
qa_results.stakeholders: Adults with hearing impairment, licensed audiologists, health insurance carriers, and insured individuals or enrollees.
qa_results.fiscal_impact_summary: Minimal special fund revenue increase for the Maryland Insurance Administration in FY 2025 from $125 rate and form filing fees, with form reviews handled using existing resources. There is no effect on the State Employee and Retiree Health and Welfare Benefits Program and no material impact on local government finances.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: MIA is the primary regulator of private commercial health insurers and HMOs in Maryland. The bill amends the Insurance Article to mandate adult hearing aid coverage, requiring MIA to review updated carrier policy form filings and collect related filing fees.

DBM administers the State Employee and Retiree Health and Welfare Benefits Program. While the state plan already covers hearing aids for adults and incurs no additional fiscal impact, DBM monitors health benefit mandates affecting state employee coverage.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Governor's Office of the Deaf and Hard of Hearing
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: ODHH coordinates state policy and advocates for the health, welfare, and accessibility needs of deaf and hard-of-hearing Marylanders, making the expansion of insurance coverage for hearing aids highly relevant to its mission.
MHBE oversees qualified health benefit plans sold on the individual and small group exchange, where state insurance mandates and Essential Health Benefit benchmark standards apply.

qa_results.bill_summary: Repeals the monopoly of the Wicomico County Liquor Control Board and its dispensaries over the wholesale sale and distribution of liquor and high-ABV wine, authorizing Class A, B, C, and D alcoholic beverages license holders in Wicomico County to purchase alcoholic beverages directly from either a dispensary or a licensed wholesaler.
qa_results.responsible_party: Liquor Control Board for Wicomico County
qa_results.stakeholders: Holders of Class A, B, C, and D alcoholic beverages licenses in Wicomico County, licensed alcohol wholesalers, and the Wicomico County Liquor Control Board and its dispensaries.
qa_results.fiscal_impact_summary: State operations and finances are not materially affected. Wicomico County revenues will decrease to the extent retail license holders choose to purchase wine and liquor through licensed wholesalers instead of the county dispensary system; the exact revenue reduction cannot be estimated at this time. Enforcement activities can be handled with existing county resources.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The Comptroller of Maryland regulates the alcohol industry and issues state wholesaler's licenses (under Title 2, Subtitle 3 of the Alcoholic Beverages and Cannabis Article, cited directly in the bill). The bill alters the distribution channels by permitting licensed wholesalers to sell and deliver liquor directly to retail licensees in Wicomico County.

qa_results.bill_summary: Authorizes Class B beer, wine, and liquor license holders in Wicomico County to purchase liquor for retail sale from licensed wholesalers in addition to the county dispensary, and allows Class B restaurant license holders who also hold a Class 9 limited distillery license to sell their manufactured products for on- and off-premises consumption.
qa_results.responsible_party: Wicomico County Board of License Commissioners
qa_results.stakeholders: Class B beer, wine, and liquor licensees (hotels and restaurants) in Wicomico County, Class 9 limited distillery licensees, licensed alcohol wholesalers, and the Wicomico County dispensary.
qa_results.fiscal_impact_summary: State effect: None. Local effect: Wicomico County can handle enforcement within existing resources; however, county revenues decrease to an indeterminate extent if licensees purchase liquor from licensed wholesalers rather than through the county dispensary.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The Comptroller is responsible for collecting state alcoholic beverage taxes and has regulatory oversight of the alcohol industry. The bill alters how alcoholic beverages are purchased and distributed at the wholesale and retail levels in Wicomico County, though it has no direct state fiscal effect.

qa_results.bill_summary: Authorizes the governing body of Howard County to enter into payment in lieu of taxes (PILOT) agreements with owners of real property who agree to maintain moderate-income housing units exceeding the minimum required by local zoning laws. It requires the County Executive to publish the methodology used to calculate the negotiated payments on the county website, reevaluate it at least once every five years, and prohibits entering into agreements not calculated according to the most recently published methodology.
qa_results.responsible_party: Howard County Executive and the governing body of Howard County
qa_results.stakeholders: Howard County government, residential property owners and housing developers, and moderate-income households seeking housing in Howard County
qa_results.fiscal_impact_summary: State effect: None. Local effect: Howard County property tax revenues may decrease beginning in FY 2025 to the extent that certain moderate-income housing developments receive property tax exemptions; however, revenue losses will be mitigated by negotiated PILOT payments. The net fiscal impact is indeterminate as it depends on the number of participating developments and their assessed values.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill authorizes Howard County to enter into payment in lieu of taxes (PILOT) agreements to promote and maintain moderate-income housing. While this is a local authorization administered by Howard County without direct state fiscal impact, it relates to the Department of Housing and Community Development's broader mission of expanding access to affordable and moderate-income housing across Maryland.

qa_results.bill_summary: Requires the Department of Natural Resources and Baltimore City to convene focus groups regarding the establishment of Gwynns Falls State Park, develop a prioritized list of park needs and associated cost assessments, establish a stakeholder advisory committee, and submit a report to the Maryland General Assembly by December 1, 2025, detailing suitable park properties and required funding.
qa_results.responsible_party: Department of Natural Resources
qa_results.stakeholders: Baltimore City residents, local park visitors, neighborhood organizations bordering the park, and local environmental and historic preservation advocacy organizations.
qa_results.fiscal_impact_summary: State general/special fund expenditures may increase by up to $70,000 in FY 2025 and up to $30,000 in FY 2026 (a maximum of $100,000) if DNR hires a consultant to assist with priority needs and cost assessments. No direct impact on revenues. Baltimore City is assumed to implement the bill using existing budgeted resources.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill directly mandates that the Department of Natural Resources (DNR), in partnership with Baltimore City, convene focus group meetings, establish a stakeholder advisory committee, develop a priority needs and cost assessment list, and submit a comprehensive report to the General Assembly regarding the proposed Gwynns Falls State Park. DNR also incurs fiscal expenditures for potential consultant services.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Executive Commissions, Committees, Task Forces, and Advisory Boards
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill creates a statutory stakeholder advisory committee to advise DNR and Baltimore City on the scope, needs, and management of the proposed Gwynns Falls State Park.

qa_results.bill_summary: This bill alters the composition of the seven-member State Board of Cosmetologists by adding one licensed esthetician and decreasing the number of consumer members from two to one.
qa_results.responsible_party: State Board of Cosmetologists, Maryland Department of Labor
qa_results.stakeholders: Licensed estheticians, consumer representatives, members of the State Board of Cosmetologists, and cosmetology industry professionals.
qa_results.fiscal_impact_summary: Altering the membership of the board does not affect State operations or finances, and has no local fiscal impact.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The State Board of Cosmetologists is administratively housed and operated within the Maryland Department of Labor, which oversees professional licensing boards.
The Governor is statutorily responsible for appointing the members of the State Board of Cosmetologists with the advice of the Secretary of Labor.

The Office of Appointments assists the Governor in recruiting, vetting, and processing gubernatorial appointments to state boards and commissions, including the newly required licensed esthetician member.

qa_results.bill_summary: Establishes a Class DBR brewery license and a Class DDS distillery permit in Frederick County, allowing eligible Class 5 breweries and Class 1 distilleries to serve as on-premises consumption permittees and sell food, nonalcoholic beverages, and their manufactured alcoholic beverages for on- and off-premises consumption.
qa_results.responsible_party: Frederick County Board of License Commissioners
qa_results.stakeholders: Class 5 breweries, Class 1 distilleries, patrons of breweries and distilleries in Frederick County, and the Frederick County Board of License Commissioners.
qa_results.fiscal_impact_summary: State effect is none. Local revenues for Frederick County may increase depending on the annual license and permit fees set and charged by the board. Enforcement activities can be absorbed with existing county budgeted resources.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill references state manufacturer licenses (Class 1 distillery and Class 5 brewery licenses) and authorizes local Frederick County permits for those license holders. The Comptroller regulates the alcohol industry and state-level alcohol manufacturer licensing in Maryland, though implementation of these specific local permits is handled by the Frederick County Board of License Commissioners with no state fiscal impact.

qa_results.bill_summary: This bill requires the Maryland State Department of Education (MSDE) to develop guidelines for an evidence-based antibias training program for school employees that addresses cultural awareness, implicit bias, and discrimination against historically marginalized racial, ethnic, and religious groups. Each local board of education must develop or update its own antibias training program based on these guidelines and provide paid, job-embedded professional development training every other year to public school employees whose duties include frequent student interaction.
qa_results.responsible_party: Maryland State Department of Education (MSDE)
qa_results.stakeholders: Public school employees with frequent student interaction, public school students, local boards of education, and nonpublic schools participating in State-funded programs.
qa_results.fiscal_impact_summary: State general fund expenditures increase by $100,000, likely in FY 2025, for MSDE to hire an external consultant to develop the antibias training guidelines. State revenues are unaffected. Local school system expenditures increase, likely minimally, to develop the program and provide the required paid professional development training every other year; these costs are expected to be largely absorbable within existing professional development schedules.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: HB 1386 directly requires the Maryland State Department of Education (MSDE) to develop, maintain, and periodically update guidelines for an antibias training program for school employees, resulting in an estimated state general fund expenditure of $100,000 in FY 2025.

qa_results.bill_summary: This bill prohibits noncompete and conflict of interest clauses in employment contracts for licensed veterinary practitioners and technicians, as well as for licensed health care professionals providing direct patient care who earn $350,000 or less per year (for contracts executed on or after July 1, 2025). For health care professionals earning more than $350,000, noncompete provisions cannot exceed one year or a 10-mile radius, and employers must notify patients upon request of a former employee's new practice location. Additionally, the Maryland Health Care Commission is required to hire an independent consultant to study private equity, hospital consolidation, and other market trends in Maryland's health care system.
qa_results.responsible_party: Maryland Health Care Commission
qa_results.stakeholders: Licensed health care professionals, veterinary practitioners, veterinary technicians, health care practices, veterinary employers, and patients.
qa_results.fiscal_impact_summary: State special fund expenditures increase by approximately $150,000 in FY 2025 for the Maryland Health Care Commission to contract with a private consultant to conduct the required health care market study. There is no state fiscal impact in FY 2024, revenues are unaffected, and local governments experience no material fiscal impact.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill explicitly mandates MHCC to contract with a private consultant to study the effect of private equity, consolidations, and acquisitions on the State's health care market and report recommendations by January 1, 2025, requiring an estimated $150,000 in special fund expenditures.

The bill amends the Labor and Employment Article regarding noncompete and conflict of interest clauses in employment contracts, falling within the Department of Labor's oversight of statewide labor laws and employment standards.

The bill places restrictions and prohibitions on noncompete provisions for direct patient care workers licensed under the Health Occupations Article, which are regulated by health licensing boards under MDH. In addition, MHCC operates as an independent commission within MDH.

The bill restricts noncompete clauses for veterinary practitioners and veterinary technicians licensed under Title 2, Subtitle 3 of the Agriculture Article, which is administered by the State Board of Veterinary Medical Examiners within MDA.

qa_results.bill_summary: This bill modifies Maryland public school construction funding and administration by establishing a 100% State share of eligible costs for qualifying major high school renovation projects, repealing the scheduled termination of the School Safety Grant Program, decreasing the annual mandated appropriation for the Nancy K. Kopp Public School Facilities Priority Fund from $80 million to $70 million starting in fiscal year 2027, accelerating State public-private partnership (P3) availability payments to Prince George's County to fiscal year 2025, establishing the Workgroup on the Assessment and Funding of School Facilities, and prioritizing High Point High School for capital improvement in Prince George's County.
qa_results.responsible_party: Interagency Commission on School Construction
qa_results.stakeholders: Maryland public school systems, local boards of education, public school students and staff, and local county governments (particularly Prince George's County, as well as Howard, Kent, Queen Anne's, Talbot, and Worcester counties).
qa_results.fiscal_impact_summary: State special fund expenditures increase by $54.0 million in FY 2025 due to accelerated P3 availability payments to Prince George's County. Beginning in FY 2027, special fund revenues and expenditures for the Nancy K. Kopp Public School Facilities Priority Fund decrease by $10.0 million annually, which is offset by continuing the $10.0 million annual general fund mandate for the School Safety Grant Program (resulting in no net effect on general funds). Prince George's County revenues increase by $54.0 million in FY 2025. Other local school systems will see alterations in the distribution of school construction funding and potential local matching requirements starting in FY 2025.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The IAC is the primary state agency responsible for implementing the bill's provisions, including administering the Nancy K. Kopp Public School Facilities Priority Fund and the School Safety Grant Program, overseeing and making payments under the Prince George's County P3 agreement, consulting with and staffing the new Workgroup, and reporting on AI weapon detection systems.

The bill directly amends provisions governing the Maryland Stadium Authority's administration of Built to Learn funding, its required review of the Prince George's County P3 agreement, its participation in the four-party memorandum of understanding, and its deposits into the P3 Fund.

The bill permanently continues the School Safety Grant Program by repealing its scheduled termination, a program that the IAC implements in direct consultation with the Maryland Center for School Safety, which manages the program's application process.

The Secretary of Budget and Management (or designee) is designated as a member of the newly established Workgroup on the Assessment and Funding of School Facilities. The bill also modifies state-mandated appropriations for school construction funds.

The State Superintendent of Schools (or designee) is designated as a member of the Workgroup on the Assessment and Funding of School Facilities, and the Maryland Center for School Safety operates as an independent unit within MSDE.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Executive Commissions, Committees, Task Forces, and Advisory Boards
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill formally creates the Workgroup on the Assessment and Funding of School Facilities to study how school conditions should be prioritized and incorporated into funding decisions.

The State Treasurer (or designee) serves as a member of the Workgroup on the Assessment and Funding of School Facilities, and the Treasurer is statutorily required to hold and invest moneys in the Nancy K. Kopp Public School Facilities Priority Fund.
The Secretary of General Services (or designee) is designated as a member of the newly formed Workgroup on the Assessment and Funding of School Facilities.
The Comptroller of Maryland is statutorily designated to account for the Nancy K. Kopp Public School Facilities Priority Fund.

qa_results.bill_summary: Modifies Maryland's electric distribution system planning laws by expanding the scope to the broader electric system, including transmission and modernizations. Broadens references to qualifying federal funding sources to include the Inflation Reduction Act alongside the Infrastructure Investment and Jobs Act, requires electric companies to report quarterly on federal funding applications, requires the Public Service Commission to mandate timely applications for federal funds and the use of least-cost debt, extends prevailing wage and labor standards to covered projects, and shifts the deadline for the Public Service Commission to adopt system planning regulations to December 31, 2025.
qa_results.responsible_party: Public Service Commission
qa_results.stakeholders: Electric utilities (investor-owned, cooperatives, and municipal utilities), utility contractors and construction workers, small businesses involved in utility infrastructure projects, and Maryland electricity ratepayers.
qa_results.fiscal_impact_summary: The Public Service Commission and the Maryland Energy Administration can handle the bill's requirements using existing budgeted resources. The bill does not otherwise materially affect State or local government finances or operations.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill directly mandates the Public Service Commission to adopt regulations and orders regarding electric system planning, demand-side reliability and efficiency methods, the pursuit of federal funds, and the use of least-cost debt, as well as receive quarterly reporting and submit annual reports to the General Assembly.

The bill explicitly tasks the Maryland Energy Administration with identifying federal funding sources (including the Infrastructure Investment and Jobs Act and Inflation Reduction Act), providing assistance to electric companies applying for federal funds, and receiving quarterly reports from electric companies.

The bill amends the Labor and Employment Article to adjust prevailing wage, apprenticeship program participation, and labor standards requirements for electric company infrastructure projects receiving federal funds, which fall under the regulatory and enforcement purview of the Department of Labor.

The Office of the People's Counsel represents residential utility consumers in proceedings before the Public Service Commission, where regulations, orders, and utility planning for electric system infrastructure, efficiency, and costs will be deliberated.

The bill broadens the electric system policy goals connected to Maryland's greenhouse gas reduction goals under the Climate Solutions Now Act, and MDE coordinates with utility providers, the PSC, and MEA regarding federal funding under related provisions.

qa_results.bill_summary: Alters numerous provisions of Maryland law prohibiting discrimination across various sectors—including employment, credit transactions, health care, housing, education, public utilities, and state procurement—to consistently include sexual orientation, gender identity, race, religious beliefs, marital status, and disability. The bill also expands the Equal Pay for Equal Work law, updates criminal law provisions regarding provocation and assault defenses, replaces statutory references to "gender" with "sex", and withdraws and repeals Chapter 244 of the Acts of 2023.
qa_results.responsible_party: Maryland Department of Labor
qa_results.stakeholders: Maryland workers, employers (including small businesses), credit applicants, lenders, health care providers and patients, public school personnel and students, and individuals protected against discrimination based on sexual orientation, gender identity, race, religious beliefs, marital status, and disability.
qa_results.fiscal_impact_summary: State general fund expenditures may increase minimally for the Maryland Department of Labor to handle a potential increase in complaints under the expanded Equal Pay for Equal Work provisions and provide training and educational materials. The bill is not anticipated to materially affect local government finances or operations.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The Maryland Commission on Civil Rights is the primary state entity responsible for enforcing anti-discrimination laws across employment, housing, public accommodations, and state contracting, which are directly amended and expanded under this act.

The bill expands protected characteristics under the State's Equal Pay for Equal Work law within the Labor and Employment Article, directly impacting the Maryland Department of Labor's enforcement duties, complaint processing volume, and training operations.

The Office of the Attorney General provides legal counsel and brings statutory civil enforcement actions under the Equal Pay for Equal Work Act and other state nondiscrimination provisions updated by the bill.
The Office of Administrative Hearings adjudicates contested discrimination cases and administrative appeals referred by the Maryland Commission on Civil Rights and other state agencies.

The bill amends the Insurance Article to prohibit health insurance carriers and health networks from discriminating against participating providers or enrollees based on expanded protected categories.

The bill amends the Public Utilities Article to prohibit electricity suppliers regulated by the Public Service Commission from discriminating against customers based on gender identity, disability, or sexual orientation.

The bill amends the Health - General and Health Occupations Articles to prohibit discrimination by home health agencies, HMOs, and licensed health practitioners on the basis of newly specified protected characteristics.
The bill amends the Education Article regarding nondiscrimination in public school employment, student course enrollment, and library employee organizations.

As the state's central procurement authority, DGS must ensure standard contract terms and bidder certifications incorporate the amended Commercial Nondiscrimination Policy under the State Finance and Procurement Article.
The bill amends the Courts and Judicial Proceedings Article to prohibit excluding citizens from jury service on the basis of sexual orientation or gender identity.
The bill amends provisions governing mandatory contract terms for provider facilities contracted by the department to expand the Resident's Bill of Rights protected categories.
The Board of Public Works oversees state procurement policies and regulations, which are modified by the bill's updates to state contracting nondiscrimination clauses and policies.

qa_results.bill_summary: Establishes the right of nonprobationary employees of the Montgomery County State's Attorney's Office, including nonsupervisory assistant State's Attorneys, to organize and collectively bargain for compensation, pensions, fringe benefits, hours, and other employment terms, while making them subject to the county merit system and personnel regulations.
qa_results.responsible_party: Montgomery County State's Attorney's Office and Montgomery County Executive
qa_results.stakeholders: Nonprobationary employees and nonsupervisory assistant State's Attorneys in the Montgomery County State's Attorney's Office, Montgomery County Government, and Montgomery County taxpayers
qa_results.fiscal_impact_summary: State Effect: None. Local Effect: Montgomery County expenditures increase to conduct collective bargaining and may increase, potentially significantly, to the extent that wages and benefits rise under a bargained agreement. For illustrative purposes, every 1% increase in personnel costs for nonsenior positions increases county expenditures by $183,000 annually, and traditional overtime provisions could cost over $2,000,000 per year. County revenues are unaffected.

qa_results.bill_summary: Expands the definition of "public school employee" for collective bargaining purposes in Dorchester County to include supervisory noncertificated employees who responsibly direct the work of other employees.
qa_results.responsible_party: Dorchester County Public Schools
qa_results.stakeholders: Supervisory noncertificated employees in Dorchester County public schools, local employee bargaining organizations, and Dorchester County Public Schools administration.
qa_results.fiscal_impact_summary: The bill has no effect on State finances and does not materially affect Dorchester County finances.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The Public Employee Relations Board (PERB) administers and oversees collective bargaining, unit clarification, representation, and labor disputes for local public school system personnel in Maryland.
The Maryland State Department of Education (MSDE) oversees Maryland's public school system, governing statutes in the Education Article concerning school system personnel classifications.

qa_results.bill_summary: This bill modifies several provisions of the Blueprint for Maryland's Future. Key changes include extending National Board Certification fee assistance to nonclassroom teachers such as principals and instructional specialists; transferring approval of career ladder classroom-time phase-in plans to the State Board of Education; authorizing multiyear planning and development funding for Judy Centers and Patty Centers; extending the phase-out of the Prekindergarten Expansion Grant Program through fiscal year 2029; permitting limits on higher education dual enrollment courses from fiscal years 2025 through 2027; altering reporting dates for the Career and Technical Education Committee; and providing temporary flexibility for the Kindergarten Readiness Assessment in the 2024–2025 school year.
qa_results.responsible_party: Maryland State Department of Education
qa_results.stakeholders: Nonclassroom educators and administrators, public school teachers, prekindergarten and kindergarten students and their families, dually enrolled high school students, local school systems, and early childhood education providers.
qa_results.fiscal_impact_summary: State special fund expenditures increase by an indeterminate amount beginning in FY 2024 to cover two-thirds of National Board Certification fees for nonclassroom teachers (estimated at approximately $82,000 in the first year and $280,000 to under $300,000 annually thereafter, though full participation could reach $4.8 million). Local school systems incur the one-third matching cost, estimated at around $140,000 annually (up to $2.4 million at full participation). Extending the Prekindergarten Expansion Grant Program through FY 2029 is assumed to be funded at $26.6 million annually, offsetting full-day prekindergarten funding and creating indeterminate secondary impacts on local share requirements, Education Effort Adjustments, and Guaranteed Tax Base aid. Limiting dual enrollment courses may reduce local school system tuition costs.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: MSDE and the State Board of Education are the primary implementing entities for the bill's changes to the Blueprint for Maryland's Future, including oversight of Judy Centers and Patty Centers, career ladder specifications, National Board Certification fee funding for nonclassroom teachers, Prekindergarten Expansion Grants, dual enrollment limits, and Kindergarten Readiness Assessment timelines.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Executive Commissions, Committees, Task Forces, and Advisory Boards
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill directly modifies authorities and deadlines for key Blueprint entities, including the Accountability and Implementation Board (AIB) and the Career and Technical Education (CTE) Committee, adjusting reporting deadlines and joint authorities on dual enrollment limits.

Local departments of social services under DHS are mandated to provide notice of prekindergarten eligibility to parents applying for economic services and must provide contact information of those parents to local school systems.
Local health departments overseen by MDH are required to notify parents applying for services about prekindergarten eligibility and share parent contact information with local school systems.

The bill references registered apprenticeship programs approved by the Division of Workforce Development and Adult Learning within the Maryland Department of Labor for attaining statewide Career and Technical Education goals.

qa_results.bill_summary: House Bill 1439 increases the annual motor vehicle registration emergency medical system surcharge from $17.00 to $40.00, distributing the funds among the Maryland Emergency Medical System Operations Fund, the Maryland Trauma Physician Services Fund, and the R Adams Cowley Shock Trauma Center. It alters reimbursement methodologies and allowable on-call rates for trauma centers and practitioners, increases maximum fines for certain impaired driving offenses (directing at least 20% of those collections to the Trauma Physician Services Fund), and establishes a mandated annual appropriation of at least $16.5 million for the Senator William H. Amoss Fire, Rescue, and Ambulance Fund beginning in fiscal year 2026.
qa_results.responsible_party: Maryland Health Care Commission and Maryland Department of Transportation Motor Vehicle Administration
qa_results.stakeholders: Maryland motor vehicle owners, trauma centers and specialty referral centers, trauma physicians and trauma health care practitioners, emergency medical services providers, local fire/rescue/ambulance departments, and drivers convicted of impaired driving offenses.
qa_results.fiscal_impact_summary: State special fund revenues increase by approximately $104.8 million annually starting in FY 2025 from the $23 vehicle registration surcharge increase (distributed among MEMSOF up to $45.6 million, Shock Trauma at least $41.0 million, and MTPSF $18.2 million). MTPSF revenues also increase by fine diversions from impaired driving violations. State special fund expenditures increase by $3.41 million in FY 2025 and $4.91 million annually thereafter due to Transportation Trust Fund credit card processing fees ($2.2 million), pediatric trauma center grants ($1.2 million), and an increased appropriation to the Amoss Fund ($1.5 million starting in FY 2026). General fund expenditures increase by $18,543 in FY 2025 for Judiciary programming, with minimal decreases in State and local fine revenues. Local governments benefit from increased grant allocations through the Amoss Fund.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: Jointly administers the Maryland Trauma Physician Services Fund with HSCRC, develops the reimbursement methodology, awards annual grants to pediatric trauma centers, and submits annual reports to the General Assembly.

Jointly administers the Maryland Trauma Physician Services Fund with MHCC, assists in developing reimbursement guidelines and on-call parameters, and tracks hospital costs accounted for in hospital global budgets.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Maryland Institute for Emergency Medical Services Systems
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: Designates trauma centers, defines the State trauma registry used to determine reimbursement eligibility, consults on trauma center grant processes, and is a major recipient of funding from the Maryland Emergency Medical System Operations Fund.
Responsible for collecting the vehicle registration emergency medical system surcharge, which is increased under the bill from $17 to $40 per vehicle per year.
Parent agency of the MVA; the Transportation Trust Fund bears an estimated $2.2 million annual increase in credit card processing fees associated with collecting the increased registration surcharge.
Administers the Senator William H. Amoss Fire, Rescue, and Ambulance Fund, which receives a mandated annual appropriation of at least $16.5 million beginning in fiscal 2026 under the bill.
Statutorily responsible for administering the Maryland Emergency Medical System Operations Fund (MEMSOF), including accounting for all transactions and performing year-end reconciliations.

Receives fund transfers from the Maryland Trauma Physician Services Fund to cover the State's share of Medicaid undercompensated trauma care expenditures, and serves as the umbrella department for MHCC and HSCRC.

Impacted by alterations and increases to maximum fines for alcohol- and drug-related driving offenses, the requirement to divert at least 20% of fine collections to MTPSF, and one-time IT programming costs.

Required by statutory mandate to allocate at least $9.00 of the annual vehicle surcharge to Shock Trauma and include an annual appropriation of at least $16.5 million in the budget bill for the Amoss Fund starting in fiscal 2026.
Responsible for state budget formulation and supervising the execution of the bill's mandated annual appropriation to the Amoss Fund and allocations from MEMSOF.
Enforces impaired driving statutes affected by the increased criminal fines, and its Aviation Command is a primary beneficiary of MEMSOF funding for medically oriented operations.
